div.head: CONTENTS /x/
div.p: INTRODUCTION By the Editor.
DRAYMAN HENSCHEL (Fuhrmann Henschel) Translated by the Editor.
ROSE BERND (Rose Bernd) Translated by the Editor.
THE RATS (Die Ratten) Translated by the Editor.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: The first volume of the present edition of Hauptmann's Dramatic Works is identical in content with the corresponding volume of the German edition. In the second volume The Rats has been substituted for two early prose tales which lie outside of the scope of our undertaking. Hence these two volumes include that entire group of dramas which Hauptmann himself specifically calls social. This term must not, of course, be pressed too rigidly. Only in Before Dawn and in The Weavers can the dramatic situation be said to arise wholly from social conditions rather than from the fate of the individual. It is true, however, that in the seven plays thus far presented all characters are viewed primarily as, in a large measure, the results of their social environment. This environment is, in all cases, proportionately stressed. To exhibit it fully Hauptmann uses, beyond any other dramatist, passages which, though always dramatic in form, are narrative and, above all, descriptive in intention. The silent burden of these plays, the ceaseless implication of their fables, is the injustice and inhumanity of the social order.

Hauptmann, however, has very little of the narrow and acrid temper of the special pleader. He is content to show humanity. It is quite conceivable that the future, forgetful of the special social problems and the humanitarian cult of to-day, may view these plays as simply bodying forth the passions and events that are timeless and constant in the inevitable march of human life. The tragedies of Drayman Henschel and of Rose Bernd, at all events, stand in no need of the label of any decade. They move us by their breadth and energy and fundamental tenderness.

No plays of Hauptmann produce more surely the impression of having been dipped from the fullness of life. One does not feel that these men and women—Hanne Schäl and Siebenhaar, old Bernd and the Flamms—are called into a brief existence as foils or props of the protagonists. They led their lives before the plays began: they continue to live in the imagination long after Henschel and Rose have succumbed. How does Christopher Flamm, that excellent fellow and most breathing picture of the average man, adjust his affairs? He is fine enough to be permanently stirred by the tragedy he has earned, yet coarse enough to fall back into a merely sensuous life of meaningless pleasures. But at his side sits that exquisite monitor—his wife. The stream of their lives must flow on. And one asks how and whither? To apply such almost inevitable questions to Hauptmann's characters is to be struck at once by the exactness and largeness of his vision of men. Few other dramatists impress one with an equal sense of life's fullness and continuity,
"The flowing, flowing, flowing of the world."

The last play in this volume, The Rats, appeared in 1911, thirteen years after Drayman Henschel, nine years after Rose Bernd. A first reading of the book is apt to provoke disappointment and confusion. Upon a closer view, however, the play is seen to be both powerful in itself and important as a document in criticism and Kulturgeschichte. It stands alone among Hauptmann's works in its inclusion of two separate actions or plots—the tragedy of Mrs. John and the comedy of the Hassenreuter group. Nor can the actions be said to be firmly interwoven: they appear, at first sight, merely juxtaposed. Hauptmann would undoubtedly assert that, in modern society, the various social classes live in just such juxtaposition and have contacts of just the kind here chronicled. His real purpose in combining the two fables is more significant. Following the great example, though not the precise method, of Molière, who produced La Critique de l'École des Femmes on the boards of his theater five months after the hostile reception of L'École des Femmes, Hauptmann gives us a naturalistic tragedy and, at the same time, its criticism and defense. His tenacity to the ideals of his youth is impressively illustrated here. In his own work he has created a new idealism. But let it not be thought that his understanding of tragedy and his sense of human values have changed. The charwoman may, in very truth, be a Muse of tragedy, all grief is of an equal sacredness, and even the incomparable Hassenreuter—wind-bag, chauvinist and consistent Goetheaner—is forced by the essential soundness of his heart to blurt out an admission of the basic principle of naturalistic dramaturgy.

The group of characters in The Rats is unusually large and varied. The phantastic note is somewhat strained perhaps in Quaquaro and Mrs. Knobbe. But the convincingness and earth-rooted humanity of the others is once more beyond cavil or dispute. The Hassenreuter family, Alice Rütterbusch, the Spittas, Paul John and Bruno Mechelke, Mrs. Kielbacke and even the policeman Schierke—all are superbly alive, vigorous and racy in speech and action.

The language of the plays in this volume is again almost wholly dialectic. The linguistic difficulties are especially great in The Rats where the members of the Berlin populace speak an extraordinarily degraded jargon. In the translation I have sought, so far as possible, to differentiate the savour and quaintness of the Silesian dialect from the coarseness of that of Berlin. But all such attempts must, from their very nature, achieve only a partial success. The succeeding volumes of this edition, presenting the plays written in normal literary German, will offer a fairer if not more fascinating field of interpretation.

div.head: The Dramatic Works of Gerhart Hauptmann, Volume II
MRS. HENSCHEL.
div.p: HANNE SCHÄL (later MRS. HENSCHEL).

lg.l: Time: Toward the end of the eighteen sixties.
Scene: The "Gray Swan" hotel in a Silesian watering place.

p.hi: A room, furnished peasant fashion, in the basement of the "Grey Swan" hotel. Through two windows set high in the left wall, the gloomy light of a late winter afternoon sickers in. Under the windows there stands a bed of soft wood, varnished yellow, in which MRS. HENSCHEL is lying ill. She is about thirty-six years of age. Near the bed her little six-months-old daughter lies in her cradle. A second bed stands against the back wall which, like the other walls, is painted blue with a dark, plain border near the ceiling. In front, toward the right, stands a great tile-oven surrounded by a bench. A plentiful supply of small split kindling wood is piled up in the roomy bin. The wall to the right has a door leading to a smaller room. HANNE SCHÄL, a vigorous, young maid servant is very busy in the room. She has put her wooden pattens aside and walks about in her thick, blue stockings. She takes from the oven an iron pot in which food is cooking and puts it back again. Cooking spoons, a twirling stick and a strainer lie on the bench; also a large, thick earthenware jug with a thin, firmly corked neck. Beneath the bench stands the water pitcher. HANNE'S skirts are gathered up in a thick pad; her bodice is dark grey; her muscular arms are bare. Around the top of the oven is fastened a square wooden rod, on which long hunting stockings are hung up to dry, as well as swaddling clothes, leathern breeches and a pair of tall, water-tight boots. To the right of the oven stand a clothes press and a chest of drawers—old fashioned, gaily coloured, Silesian pieces of furniture. Through the open door in the rear wall one looks out upon a dark, broad, underground corridor which ends in a glass door with manicoloured panes. Behind this door wooden steps lead upward. These stairs are always illuminated by a jet of gas so that the panes of the door shine brightly. It is in the middle of February; the weather without is stormy.
FRANZ, a young fellow in sober coachman's livery, ready to drive out, looks in.

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: Hanne!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Eh?

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: Is the missis asleep?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: What d'you suppose? Don't make so much noise!

lg.l: There's doors enough slammin' in this house. If that don't wake her up—!
I'm goin' to drive the carriage to Waldenburg.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Who's goin'?

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: The madam. She's goin' to buy birthday presents.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Whose birthday is it?

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: Little Karl's.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Great goin's on—those. To hitch up the horses on account o' that fool of a kid an' travel to Waldenburg in such weather!

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: Well, I has my fur coat!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Those people don't know no more how to get rid o' their money! We got to slave instead!

p.hi: In the passage appears, slowly feeling his may, the veterinarian GRUNERT. He is a small man in a coat of black sheep's fur, cap and tall boots. He taps with the handle of his whip against the door post in order to call attention to his presence.

div.head: GRUNERT
div.p: Isn't Henschel at home yet?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: What's wanted of him?

div.head: GRUNERT
div.p: I've come to look at the gelding.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: So you're the doctor from Freiburg, eh? Henschel, he's not at home. He went to Freiburg carryin' freight; seems to me you must ha' met him.

div.head: GRUNERT
div.p: In which stall do you keep the gelding?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: 'Tis the chestnut horse with the white star on his face, I believe they put him in the spare stall. [To FRANZ.] You might go along an' show him the way.

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: Just go straight across the yard, 's far as you can, under the big hall, right into the coachman's room. Then you c'n ask Frederic; he'll tell you!
[Exit GRUNERT.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Well, go along with him.

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: Haven't you got a few pennies change for me?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: I s'pose you want me to sell my skin on your account?

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: [Tickling her.] I'd buy it right off.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Franz! Don't you—! D'you want the woman to wake up? You don't feel reel well, do you, if you can't wring a few farthings out o' me! I'm fair cleaned out. [Rummaging for the money.] Here! [She presses something into his hand.] Now get out!
[The bell rings.

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: [Frightened.] That's the master. Good-bye.
[He goes hastily.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Has waked up and says weakly.] Girl! Girl! Don't you hear nothin'?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Roughly.] What d'you want?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I want you to listen when a body calls you!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: I hear all right! But if you don't talk louder I can't hear. I got only just two ears.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Are you goin' to cut up rough again?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Surly.] Ah, what do I—!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Is that right, eh? Is it right o' you to talk rough like that to a sick woman?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Who starts it, I'd like to know! You don't hardly wake up but what you begin to torment me. Nothin's done right, no matter how you do it!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: That's because you don't mind me!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: You better be doin' your work yourself. I slaves away all day an' half o' the night! But if things is that way—I'd rather go about my business!
[She lets her skirts fall and runs out.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Girl! Girl!—Don't do that to me! What is it I said that was so bad? O Lord, O Lord! What'll happen when the men folks comes home? They wants to eat! No, girl … girl!
[She sinks back exhausted, moans softly, and begins to rock her baby's cradle by means of a cord which is within her reach.

p.hi: Through the glass door in the rear KARLCHEN squeezes himself in with some difficulty. He carries a dish full of soup and moves carefully and timidly toward MRS. HENSCHEL'S bed. There he sets down the dish on a wooden chair.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Eh, Karlchen, is that you! Do tell me what you're bringin' me there?

div.head: KARLCHEN
div.p: Soup! Mother sends her regards and hopes you'll soon feel better and that you'll like the soup, Mrs. Henschel.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Eh, little lad, you're the best of 'em all. Chicken soup! 'Tis not possible. Well, tell your mother I thank her most kindly. D'you hear? Don't go an' forget that! Now I'll tell you somethin', Karlchen! You c'n do me a favour, will you? See that rag over there? Get on this bench, will you, an' pull the pot out a bit. The girl's gone off an' she put it too far in.

div.head: KARLCHEN
div.p: [After he has found the rag mounts the bench cheerfully and looks into the oven. He asks:] The black pot or the blue one, Mrs. Henschel?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: What's in the blue pot?

div.head: KARLCHEN
div.p: Sauerkraut.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Agitated.] Pull it out! That'll be boilin' to nothin'!—Eh, what a girl, what a girl!

div.head: KARLCHEN
div.p: [Has pulled the pot in question forward.] Is this right?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: You c'n let it stand that way! Come here a bit now an' I'll give you a piece o' whip cord. [She takes the cord from the window-sill and gives it to him.] An' how is your mother?

div.head: KARLCHEN
div.p: She's well. She's gone to Waldenburg to buy things for my birthday.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I'm not well, myself. I think I'm goin' to die!

div.head: KARLCHEN
div.p: Oh, no, Mrs. Henschel!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Yes, yes, you c'n believe me; I'm goin' to die. For all I care you can say so to your mother.

div.head: KARLCHEN
div.p: I'm goin' to get a Bashly cap, Mrs. Henschel.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Yes, yes, you c'n believe me. Come over here a bit. Keep reel still an' listen. D'you hear how it ticks? D'you hear how it ticks in the rotten wood?

div.head: KARLCHEN
div.p: [Whose wrist she holds in her fevered grasp.] I'm afraid, Mrs. Henschel.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Oh, never mind. We all has to die! D'you hear how it ticks? Do you? What is that? 'Tis the deathwatch that ticks. [She falls back.] One … two … one …—Oh, what a girl, what a girl!

p.hi: KARLCHEN, released from her grasp, withdraws timidly toward the door. When his hand is on the knob of the glass door a sudden terror overtakes him. He tears the door open and slams it behind him with such force that the panes rattle. Immediately thereupon a vigorous cracking of whips is heard without. Hearing this noise MRS. HENSCHEL starts up violently.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: That's father comin'!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Out in the hallway and yet unseen.] Doctor, what are we goin' to do with the beast?
[He and the veterinarian are visible through the doorway.

div.head: GRUNERT
div.p: He won't let you come near him. We'll have to put the twitch on him, I think.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [He is a man of athletic build, about forty-five years old. He wears a fur cap, a jacket of sheep's fur under which his blue carter's blouse is visible, tall boots, green hunting stockings. He carries a whip and a burning lantern.] I don't know no more what's wrong with that beast. I carted some hard coal from the mine yesterday. I came home an' unhitched, an' put the horses in the stable, an'—that very minute—the beast throws hisself down an' begins to kick.
[He puts his long whip in a corner and hangs up his cap.

p.hi: HANNE returns and takes up her work again, although visibly enraged.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Girl, get a light!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: One thing after another!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Puts out the light in the lantern and hangs it up.] Heaven only knows what all this is comin' to. First my wife gets sick! Then this here horse drops down! It looks as if somethin' or somebody had it in for me! I bought that gelding Christmas time from Walther. Two weeks after an' the beast's lame. I'll show him. Two hundred crowns I paid.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Is it rainin' outside?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [In passing.] Yes, yes, mother; it's rainin'.—An' it's a man's own brother-in-law that takes him in that way.
[He sits down on the bench.

p.hi: HANNE has lit a tallow candle and puts it into a candle stick of tin, which she sets on the table.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: You're too good, father. That's what it is. You don't think no evil o' people.

div.head: GRUNERT
div.p: [Sitting down at the table and writing a prescription.] I'll write down something for you to get from the chemist.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: No, I tell you, if that chestnut dies on top o' everythin' else—! I don't believe God's meanin' to let that happen!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Holding out his leg to HANNE.] Come, pull off my boots for me! That was a wind that blew down here on the road from Freiburg. People tell me it unroofed the church in the lower village more'n half, [To HANNE.] Just keep on tuggin'! Can't you get it?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [To HANNE.] I don't know! You don't seem to learn nothin'!
[HANNE succeeds in pulling off one boot. She puts it aside and starts on the other.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Keep still, mother! You don't do it any better!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Pulls off the second boot and puts it aside. Then in a surly voice to HENSCHEL.] Did you bring me my apron from Kramsta?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: All the things I'm axed to keep in my head! I'm content if I c'n keep my own bit of business straight an' get my boxes safe to the railroad. What do I care about women or their apron-strings?

div.head: GRUNERT
div.p: No, you're not famous for caring about them.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: An' it'd be a bad thing if he was!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Slips on wooden pattens and rises. To HANNE.] Hurry now! Hurry! We got to get our dinner. This very day we still has to go down to the smithy.

div.head: GRUNERT
div.p: [Has finished writing his prescription, which he leaves lying on the table. He slips his note book and pencil back into his pocket and says as he is about to go:] You'll hurry this to the chemist's. I'll look in early in the morning.
[HENSCHEL sits down at the table.

p.hi: HAUFFE comes in slowly. He has wooden pattens on and leathern breeches and also carries a lighted lantern.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: That's dirty weather for you again!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: How's it goin' in the stable?

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: He's goin' to end by knockin' down the whole stall.
[He blows out the light in the lantern and hangs it up next to HENSCHEL'S.

div.head: GRUNERT
div.p: Good night to all of you. All we can do is to wait. We doctors are only human too.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: To be sure. We know that without your telling us! Good night; I hope you won't overturn. [GRUNERT goes.] Now tell me, mother, how is it with you?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Oh. I've been worritin' so much again!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: What is it that worries you?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Because for all I c'n do, I'm not able to lend a hand even.

p.hi: HANNE places a disk of dumplings and one of sauerkraut on the table; she takes forks from the table drawer and puts them on the table.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: The girl's here to do the work!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: A girl like her is that thoughtless!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Oh, we gets enough to eat an' everythin' seems to go smoothly.—If you hadn't got up out o' bed too soon the first time, you might be dancin' this day!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: O Lord, me an' dancin'. What an idea!

p.hi: HANNE has prepared three plates, putting a small piece of pork on each. She now draws up a stool for herself and sits down at the table.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: There's not much left o' the oats, neither.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I bought some yesterday; thirty sacks. Saturday a load o' hay'll come too. The feed gets dearer all the time.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: If the beasts is to work they has to eat.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: But people thinks they live on air, an' so everybody wants to cut down the carting charges.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: He said somethin' like that to me too.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Who said that—the inspector?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Who else but him? But this time he met the wrong man.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, well, I'm not sayin', but that's the end of everythin'! What's to become of us these hard times?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: The inspector of roads was here. He wants you to send him teams for the big steam roller, I believe. They're in Hinterhartau now.

p.hi: Behind the glass door MR. SIEBENHAAR is seen descending the stairs. He is little over forty. Most carefully dressed; black broadcloth coat, white waist-coat, light-coloured, English trousers—an elegance of attire derived from the style of the 'sixties. His hair, already grey, leaves the top of his head bald; his moustache, on the contrary, is thick and dark blond. SIEBENHAAR wears gold-rimmed spectacles. When he desires to see anything with exactness, he must use, in addition, a pair of eye-glasses which he slips in behind the lenses of his spectacles. He represents an intelligent type.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [Approaches the open door of the room. In his right hand he holds a candle-stick of tin with an unlit candle in it and a bunch of keys; with his left hand he shades his sensitive eyes.] Has Henschel come back yet?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Yes, Mr. Siebenhaar.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: But you're just at your dinner. I have something to do in the cellar. We can talk that matter over later.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: No, no; you needn't put nothin' off on my account. I'm through!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: In that case you'd better come up to see me. [He enters the room and lights his candle by the one which is burning on the table.] I'll only get a light here now. We're more undisturbed in my office.—How are you, Mrs. Henschel? How did you like the chicken-soup?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Oh, goodness, gracious! I clean forgot about it!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Is that so, indeed?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Discovering the dish of chicken soup.] That's true; there it stands.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: That's the way that woman is! She'd like to get well an' she forgets to eat and to drink.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [As a violent gust of wind is felt even indoors.] Do tell me: what do you think of it? My wife's driven over to Waldenburg, and the weather is getting wilder and wilder. I'm really beginning to get worried. What's your opinion?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I s'pose it sounds worse than it is.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Well, well, one shouldn't take such risks. Didn't you hear that rattling? The wind broke one of the large windows in the dining-hall looking out over the verandah. You know. It's a tremendous storm!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Who'd ha' thought it!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: That'll be costin' you a good bit again!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [Leaving the room by way of the passage to the left.] There's nothing inexpensive except death.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: He's got his bunch o' troubles like the rest of us.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: What do you think he wants o' you again, father?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Nothin'! How c'n I tell? I'll hear what he says.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I do hope he won't be askin' for money again.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Don't begin talkin' nonsense, mother.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: But if them people is as hard up as all that, why does the woman has to have a twenty shillin' hat?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: You hold your tongue! No one asked you! You poke your nose over your kneadin' board an' not into other folks' affairs! It takes somethin' to keep a hotel like this goin'. Two months in the year he makes money. The rest o' the time he has to do the best he can.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: An' he had to go an' build atop o' that!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: An' 'twas that as got him in worse'n ever. He should ha' let it be.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Women don't understand nothin' o' such affairs. He had to build; he couldn't do no different. We gets more an' more people who come here for their health nowadays; there wasn't half so many formerly. But in those times they had money; now they wants everythin' for nothin'. Get the bottle. I'd like to drink a nip o' whiskey.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: [Slowly clasping his knife and getting ready to rise.] Forty rooms, three big halls, an' nothin' in 'em excep' rats an' mice. How's he goin' to raise the interest?
[He rises.

p.hi: FRANZISKA WERMELSKIRCH peeps in. She is a pretty, lively girl of sixteen. She wears her long, dark hair open. Her costume is slightly eccentric: the skirts white and short, the bodice cut in triangular shape at the neck, the sash long and gay. Her arms are bare above the elbows. Around her neck she wears a coloured ribbon from which a crucifix hangs down.

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: [Very vivaciously.] Wasn't Mr. Siebenhaar here just now? I wish you a pleasant meal, ladies and gentlemen! I merely took the liberty of asking whether Mr. Siebenhaar hadn't been here just now?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Gruffly.] We don't know nothin'. He wasn't with us!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: No? I thought he was!
[She puts her foot coquettishly on the bench and ties her shoe strings.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Mr. Siebenhaar here an' Mr. Siebenhaar there! What are you always wantin' of the man?

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: I? nothing! But he's so fond of gooseliver. Mama happens to have some and so papa sent me to tell him so.—By the way, Mr. Henschel, do you know that you might drop in to see us again, too!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: You just let father bide where he is! That'd be a fine way! He's not thinkin' about runnin' into taverns these days.

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: We're broaching a new keg to-day, though.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [While HAUFFE grins and HANNE laughs.] Mother, you stick to your own affairs. If I should want to go an' drink a glass o' beer I wouldn't be askin' nobody's consent, you c'n be sure.

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: —How are you anyhow, Mrs. Henschel?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Oh, to-morrow I'll be gettin' me a sash too an' take to rope-dancin'.

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: I'll join you. I can do that splendidly. I always practice on the carriage shafts.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: So that's the reason why all the shafts are bent!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: Do you see, this is the way it's done; this is the way to balance oneself. [Imitating the movements of a tight rope dancer, she prances out by the door.] Right leg! Left leg! Au revoir!
[Exit.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: [Taking down his lantern.] She'll go off her head pretty soon if she don't get no husband.
[Exit.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: If she had to lend a hand an' work good an' hard, she'd get over that foolishness.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: She's not allowed to come upstairs. Mrs. Siebenhaar won't have her.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: An' she's right there. I wouldn't bear it neither.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: She's always chasin' an' sniffin' around Mr. Siebenhaar. I'm willin' people should please theirselves. But she's goin' it hard.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: The Siebenhaars ought to put them people out. The goin's on with the men an' the wenches.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Aw, what are you talkin' about, mother?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, in the tap room.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, they has to live same as anybody. D'you want to see 'em put in the streets? Wermelskirch's not a bad fellow at all.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: But the woman's an old witch.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: If he pays his rent nothin' won't happen to him on that account. An' not on account o' the girl by a long way. [He has arisen and bends over the cradle.] We've got a little thing like that here too, an' nobody's goin' to put us out for that!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Eh, that would be …! She's asleep all the time; she don't seem to want to wake up!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: There's not much strength in her.—Mother, sure you're not goin' to die!—[Taking his cap from the nail.] Hanne, I was just foolin' you a while ago. Your apron is lyin' out there in the waggon.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Eagerly.] Where is it?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: In the basket. Go an' look for it!
[HENSCHEL leaves by way of the middle door; HANNE disappears into the small adjacent room.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: So he brought her the apron after all!

p.hi: HANNE runs quickly through the room again and goes out by the middle door.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: An' he brought her the apron after all!

p.hi: SIEBENHAAR enters carefully, carrying his candle and keys as before and, in addition, two bottles of claret.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: All alone, Mrs. Henschel?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: An' he brought the apron …

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: It's me, Mrs. Henschel. Did you think it was a stranger?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I don't hardly believe …

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: I hope I didn't wake you up. It's me—Siebenhaar.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: To be sure. Yes. To be sure.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: And I'm bringing you a little wine which you are to drink. It will do you good.—Is it possible you don't recognize me?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, now, that'd be queer. You are, sure—you are our Mr. Siebenhaar. Things hasn't come to such a pass with me yet. I recognise you all right!—I don't know: has I been dreamin' or what?

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: You may have been. How are you otherwise?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: But sure enough you're Siebenhaar.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Perhaps you thought I was your husband!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I don't know … I reely can't say … I was feelin' so queer …

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Seems to me you're not lying comfortably. Let me straighten your pillows a bit. Does the doctor see you regularly?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [With tearful excitement.] I don't know how it is—they just leaves me alone. No, no, you're Mr. Siebenhaar, I know that. An' I know more'n that: you was always good to me an' you has a good heart, even if sometimes you made an angry face. I can tell you: I'm that afraid! I'm always thinkin': it don't go quick enough for him.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: What doesn't go quick enough?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Bursting into tears.] I'm livin' too long for him—! But what's to become o' Gustel?

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: But, my dear Mrs. Henschel, what kind of talk is that?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Sobbing softly to herself.] What's to become o' Gustel if I die?

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Mrs. Henschel, you're a sensible woman! And so do listen to me! If one has to lie quietly in bed, you see, the way you have had to do unfortunately—week after week—why then one naturally has all kinds of foolish thoughts come into one's head. One has all sorts of sickly fancies. But one must resist all that resolutely, Mrs. Henschel! Why, that would be a fine state of affairs, if that—! Such stuff! Put it out of your mind, Mrs. Henschel! it's folly!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Dear me, I didn't want to believe it: I know what I says!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: That's just what you don't know. That's just what, unfortunately, you don't know at present. You will simply laugh when you look back upon, it later. Simply laugh!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Breaking out passionately.] Didn't he go an' see her where she sleeps!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [Utterly astonished but thoroughly incredulous.] Who went to see whom?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Henschel! The girl!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Your husband? And Hanne? Now look here; whoever persuaded you of that is a rascally liar.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: An' when I'm dead he'll marry her anyhow!

p.hi: HENSCHEL appears in the doorway.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: You're suffering from hallucinations, Mrs. Henschel!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [In good-natured astonishment.] What's the matter, Malchen? Why are you cryin' so?

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Henschel, you mustn't leave your wife alone!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Approaches the bed in kindly fashion.] Who's doin' anythin' to you?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Throws herself in sullen rage on her other side, turning her back to HENSCHEL and facing the wall.] … Aw, leave me in peace!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: What's the meanin' o' this?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Snarling at him through her sobs.] Oh, go away from me!

p.hi: HENSCHEL, visibly taken aback, looks questioningly at SIEBENHAAR, who polishes his glasses and shakes his head.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [Softly.] I wouldn't bother her just now.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [As before.] You're wishin' me into my grave!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [To HENSCHEL, who is about to fly into a rage.] Sh! Do me the favour to keep still!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: A body has eyes. A body's not blind! You don't has to let me know everythin'. I'm no good for nothin' no more; I c'n go!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Controlling himself.] What do you mean by that, Malchen?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: That's right! Go on pretendin'!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Perplexed in the extreme.] Now do tell me—anybody …!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Things c'n go any way they wants to … I won't be deceived, an' you c'n all sneak aroun' all you want to! I c'n see through a stone wall! I c'n see you for all—yes—for all! You thinks: a woman like that is easy to deceive. Rot, says I! One thing I tell you now—If I dies, Gustel dies along with me! I'll take her with me! I'll strangle her before I'd leave her to a damned wench like that!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: But mother, what's come over you?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: You're wishin' me into my grave!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Hold on, now, hold on! Or I'll be gettin' wild!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [Warning him softly.] Be calm, Henschel. The woman is ill.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Who has overheard.] Ill? An' who was it made me ill? You two—you an' your wench!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Now I'd like to know who in the world put notions like that into your head? The girl an' I! I don't understand the whole blasted thing! I'm supposed to have dealin's with her?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Don't you fetch aprons an' ribands for her?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [With renewed perplexity.] Aprons and ribands?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Yes, aprons and ribands.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, that's the queerest thing—!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Don't you think everythin' she does right an' fine? D'you ever give her a angry word? She's like the missis of the house this very day.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Mother, keep still: I'm advisin' you!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: 'Tis you that has to keep still, 'cause there's nothin' you c'n say!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [Standing by the bed.] Mrs. Henschel, you must collect yourself! All this you're saying is the merest fancy!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: You're no better'n he; you don't do no different! An' the poor women—they dies of it! [Dissolved in self-pitying tears.] Well, let 'em die!

p.hi: SIEBENHAAR gives a short laugh with an undertone of seriousness, steps up to the table and opens one of the bottles of wine resignedly.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Sitting on the edge of the bed speaks soothingly] Mother, mother—you turn over now an' I'll say a word to you in kindness. [He turns her over with kindly violence.] Look at it this way, mother: You've been havin' a dream. You dreamed—that's it! Our little dog, he dreams queer things too now an' then. You c'n see it. But now wake up, mother! Y'understan'? The stuff you been talkin'—if a man wanted to make a load o' that the strongest freight waggon'd break down. My head's fair spinnin' with it.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [Having looked for and found a glass which he now fills.] And then you raked me over the coals too!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Don't take no offence, sir. A woman like that! A man has his troubles with her.—Now you hurry up, mother, an' get well, or some fine day you'll be tellin' me I been to Bolkenhain an' stole horses.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Here, drink your wine and try to gain some strength.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: If only a body could be sure!

p.hi: SIEBENHAAR supports her while she drinks.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: What's wrong now again?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [After she has drunk.] Could you give me a promise?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I'll give you any promise you wants.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: If I dies, would you go an' marry her?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Don't ask such fool questions.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Yes or no!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Marry Hanne? [Jestingly.] O' course I would!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I mean it—serious …!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Now I just wish you'd listen to this, Mr. Siebenhaar! What's a man to say? You're not goin' to die!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: But if I does?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I won't marry her anyhow! Now you see? An' now you know it! We can make an end o' this business.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Can you promise it?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Promise what?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: That you wouldn't go an' marry the girl!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I'll promise, too; I'm willin' to.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: An' you'll give me your hand in token?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I'm tellin' you: Yes. [He puts his hand into hers.] But now it's all right. Now don't worry me no more with such stuff.

p.hi: A beautiful forenoon in May.

The same room as in the first act. The bed, in which MRS. HENSCHEL lay, is no longer there. The window which it covered is wide open. HANNE, her face toward the window, her sleeves turned up above her elbows, is busy at the washtub.
FRANZ, his shirt-sleeves and trousers also rolled up, his bare feet in wooden pattens, comes in carrying a pail. He has been washing waggons.

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: [With awkward merriment.] Hanne, I'm comin' to see you! Lord A'mighty! Has you got such a thing as some warm water?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Angrily throwing the piece of linen which she has on the washboard back into the tub and going over to the oven.] You come in here a sight too often!

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: Is that so? What's wrong, eh?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Pouring hot water into the pail.] Don't stop to ask questions. I got no time.

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: I'm washin' waggons; I'm not idlin' neither.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Violently.] You're to leave me alone! That's what you're to do! I've told you that more'n once!

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: What am I doin' to you?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: You're not to keep runnin' after me!

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: You've forgotten, maybe, how it is with us?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: How 'tis with us? No ways; nothin'! You go you way an' I goes mine, an' that's how it is!

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: That's somethin' bran' new!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: It's mighty old to me!

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: That's how it seems.—Hanne, what's come between us!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Nothin', nothin'! Only just leave me alone!

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: Has you anythin' to complain of? I been true to you!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Oh, for all I care! That's none o' my business! Carry on with anybody you want to! I got nothin' against it!

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: Since when has you been feelin' that way?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Since the beginnin' o' time!

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: [Moved and tearful.] Aw, you're just lyin', Hanne!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: You don't need to start that way at me. 'Twon't do you no good with me! I don't let a feller like you tell me I'm lyin'! An' now I just want you to know how things is. If your skin's that thick that you can't be made to notice nothin' I'll tell you right out to your face: It's all over between us!

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: D'you really mean that, Hanne?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: All over—an' I want you to remember that.

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: I'll remember it all right! [More and more excited and finally weeping more than speaking.] You don't need to think I'm such a fool; I noticed it long before to-day. But I kept thinkin' you'd come to your senses.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: That's just what I've done.

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: It's all the way you look at it. I'm a poor devil—that's certain; an' Henschel—he's got a chest full o' money. There's one way, come to think of it, in which maybe you has come to your senses.

lg.l: You start at me with such talk an' it just makes things worse an' worse.
That's all.

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: It's not true, eh? You're not schemin' right on to be Mrs. Henschel? I'm not right, eh?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: That's my business. That don't concern you. We all has to look out for ourselves.

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: Well, now, supposin' I was to look out for myself, an' goes to Henschel an' says: Hanne, she promised to marry me; we was agreed, an' so….

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Try it, that's all I says.

div.head: FRANZ
div.p: [Almost weeping with pain and rage.] An' I will try it, too! You take care o' yourself an' I'll take care o' myself. If that's the way you're goin' to act, I c'n do the same! [With a sudden change of front.] But I don't want to have nothin' more to do with you! You c'n throw yourself at his head for all I cares! A crittur like you isn't good enough for me!
[Exit hastily.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: So it worked at last. An' that's all right.

p.hi: While HANNE continues busy at her washing, WERMELSKIRCH appears in the passage at the rear. He is a man in the fifties; the former actor is unmistakable in him. He wears a thread-bare dressing-gown, embroidered slippers, and smokes a very long pipe.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [Having looked in for a while without being noticed by HANNE.] Did you hear him cough?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Who?

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Why, a guest—a patient—has arrived upstairs.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: 'Tis time they began to come. We're in the middle of May.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [Slowly crosses the threshold and hums throatily.]

lg.l: A pulmonary subject I,
Tra la la la la, bum bum!
It can't last long until I die,
Tra la la la la, bum bum!

div.p: [HANNE laughs over her washing.] Things like that really do one good. They show that the summer is coming.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: One swallow don't make no summer, though!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [Clears a space for himself on the bench and sits down.] Where is Henschel?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Why he went down, to the cemetery to-day.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: To be sure, it's his wife's birthday. [Pause.] It was a deuce of a blow to him, that's certain.—Tell me, when is he coming back?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: I don't know why he had to go an' drive there at all. We needs the horses like anything an' he took the new coachman with him too.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: I tell you, Hanne, anger spoils one's appetite.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Well, I can't help bein' angry! He leaves everythin' in a mess. The 'bus is to leave on time! An' the one-horse carriage sticks in the mud out there an' Hauffe can't budge it! The old fellow is as stiff as a goat!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Yes, things are beginning to look busy. The chef upstairs starts in to-day. It's beginning to look up in the tap-room too.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [With a short derisive laugh.] You don't look, though, as if you had much to do!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [Taking no offence.] Oh, that comes later, at eleven o'clock. But then I'm like a locomotive engine!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: I believe you. There'll be a lot o' smoke. You won't let your pipe get cold whatever happens.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [Smiling a little.] You're pleased to be pointed in your remarks—pointed as a needle.—We've got to-day, for our table music, wait now, let me think—: First of all, a bass violin; secondly, two cellos; thirdly, two first violins and two second violins. Three first, two second, three second, two first: I'm getting mixed up now. At all events we have ten men from the public orchestra. What are you laughing at? Do you think I'm fooling you? You'll see for yourself. The bass violin alone will eat enough for ten. There'll be work enough to do!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Laughing heartily.] Of course: the cook'll have a lot to do!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [Simply.] My wife, my daughter, the whole of my family—we have to work honestly and hard.—And when the summer is over we've worked ourselves to the bone—for nothing!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: I don't see what you has to complain of. You've got the best business in the house. Your taproom don't get empty, if it's summer or winter. If I was Siebenhaar upstairs, you'd have to whistle a different tune for me. You wouldn't be gettin' off with no three hundred crowns o' rent. There wouldn't be no use comin' around me with less'n a thousand. An' then you'd be doin' well enough for yourself!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [Has arisen and walks about whistling.] Would you like anything else? You frighten me so that my pipe goes out!

p.hi: GEORGE, a young, alert, neat waiter comes very rapidly down the stairs behind the glass door, carrying a tray with breakfast service. While still behind the door he stops short, opens the door, however, and gazes up and down the passage way.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Confound it all! What's this place here?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Laughing over her tub.] You've lost your way! You has to go back!

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: It's enough, God knows, to make a feller dizzy, No horse couldn't find his way about this place.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: You've just taken service here, eh?

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Well o' course! I came yesterday. But tell me, ladies an' gentlemen! Nothin' like this has ever happened to me before. I've been in a good many houses but here you has to take along a kind o' mountain guide to find your way.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [Exaggerating the waiter's Saxonian accent.] Tell me, are you from Dresden, maybe?

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Meissen is my native city.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [As before.] Good Lord A'mighty, is that so indeed?

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: How do I get out of here, tell me that!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Alert, mobile, and coquettish in her way in the waiter's presence.] You has to go back up the stairs. We has no use down here for your swallow tails.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: This is the first story, eh? Best part o' the house?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: You mean the kennels or somethin' like that? We'll show you—that we will! The very best people live down here!

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: [Intimately and flirtatiously.] Young woman, do you know what? You come along an' show me the way? With you I wouldn't be a bit afraid, no matter where you lead me to. I'd go into the cellar with you or up into the hay loft either.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: You stay out o' here! You're the right kind you are! We've got enough of your sort without you.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Young woman, do you want me to help with the washin'?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: No! But if you're aimin' at it exackly, I c'n help you to get along! [Half drawing a piece of linen out of the suds.] Then you'd be lookin' to see where your starched shirt-front went to!

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: O dear! You're not goin' to mess me up that way, are you? Well, well, that wouldn't do! We'd have to have a talk about that first! That so, young woman? Well, o' course! We'll talk about it—when I has time, later.
[He mounts the stairs and disappears.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: He won't lose his way very often after this! Siebenhaar will see to it that he gets to know the way from the dining hall to the kitchen.—Hanne, when is Henschel coming back?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: About noon, I s'pose! D'you want me to give him a message?

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Tell him—don't forget, now—tell him that I—send him my regards.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Such foolishness. I might ha' thought …!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [Passing her with a slight bow.] Thoughts are free … I wish you a good morning.
[Exit.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Alone, washing vigorously.] If only Henschel wasn't such a fool!

p.hi: Above the cellar, outside, the pedlar FABIG, kneeling down, looks in at the window.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: Good mornin', young woman! How are you? How's everythin'?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Who are you anyhow?

div.head: FABIG
div.p: Why—Fabig, from Quolsdorf. Don't you know me no more? I'm bringin' you a greetin' from your father. An' he wants me to tell you … Or maybe you'd want me to come in?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Aw, I know. I believe you. He wants money again. Well, I has none myself.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: I told him that myself. He wouldn't believe me. Are you all alone, young woman?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Why d'you ax?

div.head: FABIG
div.p: [Lowering his voice.] Well now you see, there's more'n one thing I has on my heart. An', through the window, people might be hearin' it.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Oh well, I don't care. You c'n come in! [FABIG disappears from the window.] That that feller had to be comin' to-day …!
[She dries her hands.

p.hi: FABIG enters. He is a poorly clad, strangely agile, droll pedlar, with a sparse beard, about thirty-six years old.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: A good mornin' to you, young woman.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Fiercely.] First of all, I'm no young woman but a girl.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: [With cunning.] Maybe so. But from all I hears you'll be married soon.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: That's nothin' but a pack o' mean lies—that's what it is.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: Well, that's what I heard. It's no fault o' mine. People is sayin' it all over; because Mrs. Henschel died …

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Well, they can talk for all I care. I does my work. That's all that concerns me.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: That's the best way. I does that way myself. There's little that folks hasn't said about me some time … In Altwasser they says I steals pigeons. A little dog ran after me … o' course, they said I stole it.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Well now, if you got anythin' to say to me, go ahead an' don't waste words.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: Now you see, there you are. That's what I always says too. People talks a good deal more'n they ought to. They has a few rags to sell an' they talks an' talks as if it was an estate. But I'll say just as little as possible. What I wants to tell you about, young woman—now don't fly up: the word just slipped out!—I meant to say: lass—what I wants to tell you about is your daughter.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Violently.] I has no daughter, if you want to know it. The girl that father is takin' care of, is my sister's child.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: Well now, that's different, that is. We've all been thinkin' the girl was yours. Where is your sister?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Who knows where she is? She's not fool enough to tell us. She thinks, thinks she: they c'n have the trouble an' see how they gets along.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: Well, well, well! There you see again how folks is mistaken. I'd ha' taken any oath … an' not me, not me alone, but all the folks over in Quolsdorf, that you was the mother o' that child.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Yes, I knows right well who says that o' me. I could call 'em all by name! They'd all like to make a common wench o' me. But if ever I lays my hands on 'em I'll give 'em somethin' to remember me by.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: Well, it's a bad business—all of it! Because this is the way it is: the old man, your father, I needn't be tellin' you—things is as they is—he don't hardly get sober. He just drinks in one streak. Well, now that your mother's been dead these two years, he can't leave the little thing—the girl I mean—at home no more. The bit o' house is empty. An' so he drags her around in the pubs, in all kinds o' holes, from one village taproom to the next. If you sees that—it's enough to stir a dumb beast with pity.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [With fierce impatience.] Is it my fault that he swills?

div.head: FABIG
div.p: By no means an' not at all. Nobody c'n keep your old man from doin' his way! 'Tis only on account o' the child, an' it's that makes a body feel sorry. But if that there little one can't be taken away from him an' given in the care o' decent folks, she won't live no ten weeks after this.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Hardening herself.] That don't concern me. I can't take her. I got all I can do to get along!

div.head: FABIG
div.p: You'd better come over to Quolsdorf some time an' look into it all. That'd be best, too. The little girl … 'tis a purty little thing, with bits o' hands an' feet like that much porcelain, so dainty an' delicate.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: She's not my child an' she don't concern me.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: Well, you better come over an' see what's to be done. It's hard for people to see such things goin' on. If a man goes into an inn, in the middle of the night or some time like that—I got to do that, you see, in the way o' business—an' sees her sittin' there with the old man in the midst o' tobacco smoke—I tell you it hurts a body's soul.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: The innkeepers oughtn't to serve him nothin'. If they was to take a stick an' beat him out o' their places, maybe he'd learn some sense.—A waggon's just come into the yard. Here you got a sixpence. Now you get along an' I'll be thinkin' it all over. I can't do nothin' about it this minute. But if you goes aroun' here in the inns an' talks about it—then it's all over between us.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: I'll take good care, an' it don't concern me. If it's your child or your sister's child—I'm not goin' to poke my nose in the parish register, nor I'm not goin' to say nothin' neither. But if you want a bit o' good advice,'tis this: Tell Henschel straight out how 'tis. He won't tear your head off by a long way!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [With increasing excitement as HENSCHEL'S voice grows more clearly audible.] Oh this here jabberin'! It's enough to drive you crazy.
[Exit into the adjoining room.

p.hi: HENSCHEL enters slowly and seriously. He wears a black suit, a top hat and white knitted gloves.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Remains standing and looks at FABIG with an expression of slow recollection. Simply and calmly.] Who are you?

div.head: FABIG
div.p: [Alertly.] I buy rags, waste paper, furniture, cast off clothes, anythin' that happens to be aroun'.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [After a long glance, good-naturedly but with decision.] Out with the fellow!

p.hi: FABIG withdraws with an embarrassed smile.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Takes off his top-hat and wipes his forehead and neck with a manicoloured handkerchief. Thereupon, he places his hat on the table and speaks toward the door of the next room:] Girl, where are you?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: I'm with Gustel here in the little room.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: All right. I c'n wait. [He sits down with a sigh that is almost a groan.] Yes, yes, O Lord—a man has his troubles.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Enters busily.] The dinner'll be ready this minute.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I can't eat; I'm not hungry.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Eatin' and drinkin' keeps body an' soul together. I was once in service with a shepherd, an' he said to us more'n one time: If a body has a heartache or somethin' like that, even if he feels no hunger, 'tis best to eat.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, cook your dinner an' we'll see.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: You shouldn't give in to it. Not as much as all that. You got to resign yourself some time.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Was that man Horand, the bookbinder, here?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Everythin's attended to. He made forty new billheads. There they are on the chest.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Then the work an' the worry begins again. Drivin' in to Freiburg mornin' after mornin' an' noon after noon haulin' sick people across the hills.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: You're doin' too much o' the work yourself. Old Hauffe is too slow by half. I can't help it—if I was you I'd get rid o' him.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Gets up and goes to the window.] I'm sick of it—of the whole haulin' business. It c'n stop for all I care. I got nothin' against it if it does. To-day or to-morrow; it's the same to me. All you got to do is to take the horses to the flayers, to chop up the waggons for kindlin' wood, an' to get a stout, strong bit o' rope for yourself.—I think I'll go up an' see Siebenhaar.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: I was wantin' to say somethin' to you when I got a chance.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, what is it, eh?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: You see, it's not easy for me. No, indeed. [Elaborately tearful.] But my brother—he needs me that bad. [Weeping.] I'll have to leave—that's sure.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [In extreme consternation.] You're not right in your mind. Don't start that kind o' business!

p.hi: HANNE, shedding crocodile tears, holds her apron to her eyes.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Well now, look here, lass: you're not goin' to play me that kind of a trick now! That would be fine! Who's goin' to manage the house? Summer's almost with us now an' you want to leave me in the lurch?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [With the same gesture.] 'Tis the little one I feels sorry for!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: If you don't take care of her, who's goin' to?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [After a space collecting herself apparently by an effort of the will. Quietly:] It can't be done no different.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Everythin' c'n be done in this world. All you needs is to want to do it.—You never said nothin' about it before. An' now, suddenly, you talk about your brother!—Maybe I been offendin' you some way? Don't you feel suited with me no more?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: There's no end to the gossip that's goin' round.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: What kind o' gossip?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Oh, I don't know. I'd rather be goin out o' the way of it.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I'd like to know just what you mean!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: I does my work an' I takes my pay! An' I won't have nobody say such things o' me. When the wife was still alive I worked all day; now that she's dead, I don't do no different. People c'n say all they wants to; I'm tryin' to make you think I'm fine, an' I want dead people's shoes. I'd rather go into service some other place.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Relieved.] You needn't say no more if that's all it is!

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Takes up some piece of work as an excuse for leaving the room.] No, no, I'll go. I can't never stay!
[Exit.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Talking after her.] You c'n let people talk an' not say much yourself. All them tongues has to wag for an occupation. [He takes off his black coat and hangs it up. Sighing.] The pack o' troubles don't get no smaller.

p.hi: SIEBENHAAR comes in slowly. He carries a decanter full of water and a glass.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Good morning, Henschel.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Good mornin' Mr. Siebenhaar,

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Am I disturbing you?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Not a bit; not at all. You're very welcome.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [Placing the decanter and the glass on the table.] I've got to drink the medicinal spring water again. I'm having that old trouble with my throat. Well, dear me, a man has to die of something!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: You must just go ahead an' drink the waters. They'll cure you.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Yes, that's just what I'm doing.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: An' not from the Mill Spring nor from the Upper Spring. Ours is the best.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Well now, to change the subject. [Half lost in thought he has been toying with a sprig of ivy. Now he observes this, starts slightly, runs his eyes over the top-hat and HENSCHEL himself and says suddenly:] This was your wife's birthday, wasn't it?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: She'd ha' been thirty-six years old to-day.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Is it possible?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Oh, yes, yes.
[Pause.]

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Henschel, I'd better leave you alone now. But when it's agreeable to you—to-morrow maybe, I'd like to talk over some business with you.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I'd rather you went ahead right now.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: It's about the thousand crowns …

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Before we says any more, Mr. Siebenhaar. You c'n just keep that money till winter. Why should I be lyin' to you? You see? I don't need the money. I don't care exackly when I gets it; an' that it's safe, I'm satisfied o' that.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Well, Henschel, in that case I'm very grateful to you. You're doing me a great favour. During the summer I take in money; you know that. Just now it would have been difficult for me.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, you see, so we c'n agree fine.
[Pause.]

div.head: SIEBENHAAR.
div.p: [Walking to and fro.] Yes, yes, I sometimes wonder over myself. I grew up in this house. And yet, to-day, if I could but make a decent closing out, I could leave it quite calmly.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I wouldn't like to go, I must say. I wouldn't hardly know where to go to.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Things have moved ahead with you, Henschel. But the same set of conditions that has counted in your favour, has been that against which I've had to struggle to keep my head above water.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: The shoe pinches one man in this place an' another man in that. Who's goin' to say which is worse off? You see, I got a good, hard blow, too. An' if I'm goin' to recover … well, I don't hardly feel like myself yet.
[Pause.]

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Henschel, there's a time for everything! You'll have to conquer that now. You must go out among people, hear things, see things, drink a glass of beer once in a while, plunge into business, perhaps—somehow, put an end to this sad business. It can't be helped, and so—forward!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: 'Tis just as you say! You're quite right!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: To be sure, your wife was the best, most faithful woman. There's only one opinion about that. But you are in the full current of life, Henschel; you're in your best years; you still have a great deal to do in the world: who knows how much. You needn't forget your wife on that account; on the contrary. And that's entirely out of the question in the case of a man like you. But you must honour her memory in a saner way. This kind of brooding does no good. I've been watching you for a good while and I determined, without saying anything, to make a really strong appeal to you one day. You're letting yourself be actually downed.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: But what's a man to do against it? You're right—that you are; but times I hardly know what to do! You say: Plunge into business. But there's somethin' lackin' all around. Four eyes sees better'n two; four hands—they c'n do a sight more. Now I got all these coaches here in the summer! An' there's no one to see to things at home! 'Tis not easy, I c'n tell you that.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: I thought that Hanne was quite a capable girl.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, you see, she's given me notice, too.—'Tis too hard for a man to get along without a wife. Yon can't depend on no one. That's just it; that's just what I says!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Why don't you marry, Henschel?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: 'Twould be best!—What c'n I do without a wife? A man like me can't get along without one. I was thinking in fact, of goin' upstairs an' askin' the missis if, maybe, she could give me some advice in that direction. She died an' left me alone in the midst of all these worries.—An', also, to tell you the truth, this business of mine's not what it used to be. How long is it goin' to be before the railroad comes here? Well, you see, we'd put by a little, an' we wanted to buy a small inn—maybe in two years or so. Well, that can't be done without a woman neither.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: True. You won't be able to get along this way permanently. You can't remain a widower the rest of your life. If for no other reason but for the child's sake.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: That's what I always says.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Of course I have no right to interfere in your affairs. Still, we're old friends. To wait, Henschel, just on account of what people will think—that's sheer nonsense, no more, no less. If you are quite seriously thinking of marrying again, it would be better both for you and for the child if you did it soon. You needn't be overhasty; assuredly not! But if you've quite made up your mind, then—go straight ahead! Why should you hesitate? [After a pause during which HENSCHEL scratches his head.] Have you any one particular in view?

lg.l: —If I got some one in view? That's what you'd like to know? Maybe I has.
Only I can't marry her.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: But why not?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: You know it yourself.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: I? I know it? How's that?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: All you got to do is a little thinkin'.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [Shaking his head.] I can't say that I recall at this moment.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Didn't I have to go an' promise my wife …

div.head: SIEBENHAAR.
div.p: ———?—Oh, yes!!—You mean the girl—Hanne?—
[Pause.]

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I been thinkin' an' thinkin'. There's no use in denyin' it. When I wakes up during the night, I can't sleep for a couple o' hours sometimes. I got to be thinkin' of it all the time. I can't get over it any way!—The girl's a good girl. She's a bit young for an old fellow like me, but she c'n work enough for four men. An' she's taken very kindly to Gustel; no mother could do more'n she. An' the girl's got a head on her, that's sure, better'n mine. She c'n do sums better'n I can. She might go an' be a calculator. She knows a bit o' business to the last farthing, even if six weeks have come an' gone since. I believe she could make a fool o' two lawyers.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Well, if you're so thoroughly convinced of all that …!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: There wouldn't be no better wife for me! An' yet … an' yet! I can't get over it.
[Pause.]

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: I do remember quite dimly now what you mean. It was quite at the end of her life.—But I confess to you quite frankly: I didn't take that matter so very seriously. Your wife was in a very excited condition. And that was caused largely by her illness.—I can't think that that is the main question. The real question must finally be whether Hanne is really suitable for you! She has her advantageous qualities: no doubt about that. There are things about her that I like less. However: who hasn't some faults. People say that she has a child.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: That she has. I've inquired. Well, even so. I don't care nothin' about that. Was she to wait for me, eh? She didn't know nothin' about me when that happened. She's hot-blooded; all right. That'll come out somehow. When the pears is ripe, they falls to the ground. On that account—no, that don't trouble me none.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Well, then! The other matter is trivial. Perhaps not trivial exactly. I can well understand how it's taken hold of you. Still, one must get free of it. To be bound by it, in spite of one's saner thought—that's clearly folly, Henschel.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I've said that to myself ten times over. You see, my wife she didn't never want anythin' but what was for my best good. I mean, in the days when she was well. She wouldn't want to stand in my way. Wherever she is, maybe, she'd want to see me get along.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Assuredly.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, I went out to her grave to-day. The missis had a wreath put there too. I thought to myself I'd better go there, that's what I thought. Maybe she'll be sendin' you some message. Mother, I said in my thoughts, give me a sign. Yes or no! Anyway you answers, that way it'll be! An' I stood, there half an hour.—I prayed, too, an' I put it all to her—just to myself, o' course—about the child an' the inn an' that I don't know what to do in my business—but she didn't give me no sign.

p.hi: HANNE enters throwing sidelong glances at the two men, but at once going energetically to work. She puts the washbench and tub aside and busies herself at the stove.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [To HENSCHEL.] God give the dead peace and blessedness. You are a man; you're in the midst of life. Why should you need signs and miracles? We can find our way in this world by depending with fair certainty on our reason. You simply go your way. You're captain on your own ship. Overboard with all these fancies and sickly notions! The more I think of your plan, the more rational it seems to me …

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Hanne, what do you say about it?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: I don't know. How c'n I tell what you're talkin' about?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: You just wait: I'll tell you later.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Well, good morning, Henschel. I'll see you later. Meanwhile—good luck!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I'll hope I'll have it.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: I'm not worried about you. You had a lucky way with you always.
[Exit.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Yon shouldn't be sayin' it! 'Tis bad luck.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: If you spits three times, it'll take the curse off.
[Pause.]

div.head: HANNE
div.p: I can't help thinkin' as you're too good.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: What makes you think so?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: People just robs you: that's what I says.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Did you think he wanted somethin' of me?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: Well, what else? He ought to be ashamed to come beggin' o' poor people.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Hanne, you don't know what you're sayin'.

div.head: HANNE
div.p: I knows well enough.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: That's what you don't. An' you couldn't know. But some day, later on, you'll come to understand.—Now I'll be goin' to the taproom an' buy me a mug o' beer. It'll be the first time these eight weeks. After that we c'n eat, an' after the dinner then—listen to me—then we might say a word to each other. Then we c'n see how everythin' c'n be straightened out.—Or, maybe, you don't care about it?

div.head: HANNE
div.p: You was sayin' yourself: We c'n see.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: An' that's what I says now. We c'n wait.
[Exit.
[Pause.]

div.head: HANNE
div.p: [Works on undisturbed. When HENSCHEL is out of hearing, she suddenly ceases, scarcely mastering her joyous excitement, she dries her hands and tears off her apron. In involuntary triumph:] I'll show you. Watch out!

p.hi: The same room as tn the two preceding acts.

It is evening toward the end of November. A fire is burning in the oven; a lighted candle stands on the table. The middle door is closed. Muffled dance music penetrates into the room from the upper stories of the house.
HANNE, now MRS. HENSCHEL, sits by the table and knits; she is neatly and suitably clad in a dress of blue cotton, and wears a red kerchief across her breast.
HILDEBRANT, the smith, enters. A small, sinewy person.

div.head: HILDEBRANT
div.p: Good evenin', missis, where's your husband?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Gone to Breslau. He's fetchin' three new horses.

div.head: HILDEBRANT
div.p: Then I s'pose he won't be comin' home to-day, eh?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Not before Monday.

div.head: HILDEBRANT
div.p: Well, this is Saturday.—We've brought back the board waggon. It's downstairs in the entry way. We had to renew all the four tires. Where's Hauffe?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: He hasn't been with us this long time.

lg.l: So he hasn't. 'Tis nonsense I'm talkin'. I mean the new servant. Is
Schwarzer here?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: He's gone along to Breslau.

div.head: HILDEBRANT
div.p: Fact is I knows all about Hauffe. He comes down to the smithy an' just stands aroun'. He's got nothin' to do yet.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: People says he's beginnin' to drink.

div.head: HILDEBRANT
div.p: I believes it. That's the way it goes. 'Tis bad for an old fellow like that; nobody wants him now.—What's goin' on up there to-day?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Dancin'!

div.head: HILDEBRANT
div.p: How'd it be if we was to go up there too, missis. Why shouldn't we be joinin' in a little waltz too?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: They'd open their eyes pretty wide up there if we did.—But what is it you want of Henschel?

div.head: HILDEBRANT
div.p: His honour, the judge, has a chestnut stallion that don't want to let hisself be shoed. So we wanted to ax Henschel to step over. If he can't get any beast to stand still, why then—! Well, good evenin', Mrs. Henschel.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Good evenin'.

p.hi: HILDEBRANT withdraws.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL.
div.p: [Listens to a dragging noise out in the passage.] What kind of a noise is that there? [She steps forward and opens the door.] Who's makin' all that racket out there?

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: [Comes dancing in.] Get out of the way, Mrs. Henschel! I have no time.
[She whirls about in the room to the measure of the waltz heard from above.]

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, this is a fine way to act! What's the matter with you? Did a mad dog bite you, maybe?

p.hi: FRANZISKA dances on and hums the melody of the waltz.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [More and more amused.] For heaven's sake! Somethin's goin' to happen to you!—No, girl, you're goin' clear out o' your mind!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: [Sinks exhausted into a chair as the music breaks off.] Oh, Mrs. Henschel, I could dance myself to death!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Laughing.] At this here rate I believes you! It makes a body feel dizzy just to watch you.

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: Don't you dance at all?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Me? If I dance? To be sure I do. 'Twasn't once or twice only that I got a pair o' new shoes an' danced 'em to pieces in one night!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: Come and dance with me then!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Why don't you go upstairs an' dance with the folks there?

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: Oh, if only I might! Do you know what I'll do? I'll sneak up! I'll sneak into the gallery! Have you ever been up there? The bags of prunes stand up there. I go up there quite boldly and look down, and eat prunes. Why shouldn't I look down from there?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: An' maybe Siebenhaar'll send for you to come down.

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: I just stare down as bold as you please. I don't care a bit. And whenever a lady dances with Mr. Siebenhaar, I pelt her with plum pits.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: You're crazy about Siebenhaar—that's certain!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: Well, he's a real swell—that's what none of the others are. [The music is heard again.] Ah, they're starting. That's a polka! [Dancing again.] I'd like to dance with Mr. Siebenhaar this minute. D'you know what I'd do? I'd just kiss him before he knew what was happening.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Siebenhaar'd be too old for me!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: Your husband is just as old, Mrs. Henschel.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Look here, girl, I want you to know that my husband is a good five years younger.

lg.l: Well, he looks much older anyhow. Why, he looks so old and wrinkled. No,
I wouldn't care to kiss him.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: You better see about getting out o' here, or I'll take a broom an' help you along! Don't you abuse my husband! An' where would I get a better one? You wait till you're a few years older an' you'll see what it means in this world to have a husband!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: I won't marry at all. I'll wait till some fine, rich gentleman comes—some summer—for his health—a Russian, by preference—and then I'll let him take me out into the world. I want to see the world—to wander far—I want to go to Paris. And then I'll write you about myself, Mrs. Henschel.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I do believe you'll run off some day!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: You can wager anything that I will. Mr. Siebenhaar was in Paris, too, you know, during the revolution in 'forty-eight, and he can tell you the most interesting stories! Oh, I'd like to see a revolution like that some day too. They build barricades …

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH'S VOICE
div.p: Franziska! Franziska! Where are you keeping yourself again?

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: Sh! Don't say anything!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH'S VOICE
div.p: Franziska! Franziska!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: Sh! Keep still! He wants me to serve at the bar. And that's horrid and I won't do it!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH'S VOICE
div.p: Franziska!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: It's papa's or mama's place to do that. Or they can hire a waiter. I won't be turned into a bar maid.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: That's not the worst kind o' thing!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: Oh, if there were real gentlemen to serve! But they're just well—attendants, coachmen and miners. Much obliged for such company! I don't care about it!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: If I was you, I'd do that reel easy. An' I'd be gettin' good tips. You could save a good many pennies an' put by a nice sum.

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: I won't accept pennies and farthings. And if some time Mr. Siebenhaar or the architect or Dr. Valentiner gives me a present, I spend it on sweetmeats right away.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Ah, that's just it. You're your father's daughter. An' your mother wasn't much different neither. You people don't take care o' the business you has! If you'd ha' done so you'd have money out at interest this day.

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: We're not as stingy as you, that's all.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I'm not stingy. But you got to keep your substance together.

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: People say you're stingy, though!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: People c'n be—! An' you too! Hurry now an' get out o' here! I'm sick o' your jabberin' now! An' you don't need to come back here neither! I haven't been longin' for you, exackly! 'Tis best not to see or hear anything o' the whole crowd o' you.

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: [Turning once more at the door, with angry malice.] Do you know what else people say?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I don't want to know nothin'! Get out o' here! You look out that you don't get to hear things about yourself! Who knows what's between you an' Siebenhaar? You two knows it an' I knows it too. Otherwise you'd ha' been kicked out twenty times over with your slovenly management! Teach me to know Siebenhaar!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: Fy, fy and fy again!
[Exit.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: The baggage!

p.hi: The middle door has remained open. SIEBENHAAR and the waiter GEORGE, coming from different directions along the passage way, are seen to meet at the door. GEORGE affects the height of Vienna fashions—hat, cane, long overcoat, gay tie.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: What are you after here?

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: You'll forgive me but I have some business with Drayman Henschel.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
