div.p: Henschel is not at home. You've been told three times now that there is no place for you in my house. If you can't remember that henceforth I shall be compelled to have your memory assisted by—the constable.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: I beg your pardon very humbly, Mr. Siebenhaar, but I begs to submit that I don't come to see you. These people lives in your house. An' you can't prove nothin' as touchin' the question of my honour.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Very well. Only, if I should meet you again I'll have the porter kick you out. So you had better act accordingly.
[Exit.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: [Enters the room cursing.] I'll take that there risk! We'll see about that later!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Closes the door, with difficulty mastering her rage toward SIEBENHAAR.] We're here, too, I'd have him know. Just let him try it! This here is our room, not his room, an' anybody that comes here comes to us an' not to him! He's got no right to say nothin' about it!

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: We'll just wait an' see—that's all I says. He might have to pay good an' dear for that. That kind o' thing takes a man to the pen. He got hisself into a nasty mess with Alphonse, who was here two years ago. But he'd be gettin' into a worse mess with me. A hundred crowns o' damages'd be too little for me.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: An' he hasn't got no hundred crowns in his pocket—the damned bankrupt! He's been borrowing of everybody in the county. He's got nothin' but debts; you hear that on all sides. 'Twon't be long before there won't be nothin' left an' he'll have to leave the house hisself instead o' puttin' other people out of it!

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: [Has recovered his overcoat, hung up his hat, and is now picking off the little feathers from his coat and trousers.] That's right! An' that's no secret to nobody. Even the people that come here year in an' out says the same. An' nobody is sorry for him; no, they're willin' it should happen to him. My present boss, he can't stand him neither. He gets reel venomous if you so much as mention Siebenhaar's name. [Takes a pocket-mirror and comb from his pocket and smooths his hair.] Lord knows, he says, there's more tricks to that man than a few.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I believes that; I s'ppose he's right there.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Now then, Hanne, has you got somethin' warm for me?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Why didn't you come yesterday?

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: You thinks I c'n get off every day, don't you? 'Twas hard enough to get to come here to-day! Yesterday I was busy till three o'clock in the mornin'.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL:
div.p: What was it happened?

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: There was a meetin' o' the fire board. They bought a new engine, an' so they wanted to celebrate the purchase. That's how they came to have a meetin'.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: All they wants is an excuse to swill. An' all that while I sat till late at night and waited. Once—I don't know, but it must ha' been a bird flyin' against the window—I thought 'twas you, an' so I went to the window an' opened it. After that I was that mad, I couldn't sleep half the night.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Oh, pshaw! What's the use o' havin' things like that spoil one's temper. [He puts his arms around her.] That's nothin'! Nothin' at all.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Frees herself from his embrace.] Oh, I don't know! 'Tis true—I don't know how it comes—but things seem to go contrary with a body. Henschel sits aroun' at home the whole week, an' now that he's gone for a bit, we has to let the time slide away!

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Well, we got plenty o' time to-day. He don't come back till Monday, I thought.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Who knows if it's true!

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: I don't know no reason why it shouldn't be true!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: That man is bound to sit aroun' at home. 'Twasn't half as bad formerly. He used to go on trips weeks at a time; nowadays he whines if he's got to sleep away from home a single night. An' if he says: I'll stay three days, he mostly comes back on the second—Listen … I believe they've come already! Who else'd be crackin' whips like that in the yard?

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: [After he has listened, in a restrained tone:] The devil take 'em all—the whole damned crowd! A man hasn't had time to get warm a bit. I s'pose I'll have to leave right off, eh? I thought it'd be mighty different, I must say!
[He slips his overcoat back on and takes up his hat.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Tears his hat from his head.] You stay right here! What d'you want to run off for? D'you think I got to be scared o' Henschel. He's got to come to my terms. I don't has to think about him. If you'd come yesterday!—I told you …! Then nobody wouldn't ha' interrupted us, no Henschel an' no Siebenhaar. To-day the devil's broke loose!

p.hi: The horse dealer WALTHER enters—a handsome, vigorous fellow of forty. Bashly cap, fur jacket, hunting stockings and tall boots; his mits are fastened by cords.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: Missis, your husband is outside in the yard. I'm just comin' in for a minute to bid you good evenin'. I got to ride off again straight way. He's bought some fine Flemish horses. An' he's brought along something else, for you too.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I thought he wouldn't be comin' back till Monday.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: An' that's the way it would ha' been. But we couldn't ride on horseback no farther'n Kanth. There we had to take the train with the horses or they'd ha' broken their necks an' their limbs. Travellin' was that bad on account o' the sleet.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: You makes better time with the train—that's certain!

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: What kind of a feller is that there? Why, you're tryin' to be invisible, eh? Well, if that isn't little George—I do believe! Why, you looks like a natural born baron!

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: A man earns more over there in the "Star" hotel. I has a much more profitable position. Here I had to work till my clothes dropped from me in rags. I was most naked in the end; now I'm beginnin' to buy somethin' again.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: Now guess, missis, what your husband has brought home for you!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, what is it?

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: I wager you'll be mighty glad of that present!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: We'll see. It depends on what it is.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: Good luck to you then. I got to hurry or my wife'll get ugly.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Good luck to you.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: I might as well come along. Good night, Mrs. Henschel.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Didn't you want to see Henschel about somethin'?

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: There's plenty o' time for that. There's no hurry.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: If you got somethin' to say to him you'd better wait till to-morrow. He's got different kinds o' things in his mind to-day. D'you know what he's bringin' you, missis?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: What should he be bringin' me? Don't talk so much nonsense.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: Why, he's bringin' you your daughter!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: —What's that he's bringin'? I didn't hear right!

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: We was in Quolsdorf and fetched her.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: You're drunk, the two o' ye, eh?

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: No, no, I'm tellin' you the truth.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Who did you get?

lg.l: He didn't tell me nothin' about it. All of a sudden we was in the pub at
Quolsdorf an' sat down there.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, an' what then?

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: We was sittin' there an' then, after a little while, your father came in with the bit of a girl.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: 'Tis no girl o' mine!

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: I don't know nothin' about that! I knows this much though: he's got the child out there. He went up to your father an' he said: The child's a pretty child.—Then he took her in his arms an' petted her. Shall I take you with me, he axes her, an' she was willin' right off.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, an' my father?

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: Well, your father didn't know who Henschel was!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Better an' better! An' is that all?

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: [Almost addressing GEORGE now.] No, there was nothin' more. He just took the little one out an' said to your father: I'll let the lass ride horseback. An' she kept cryin' out: Lemme ride! Lemme ride! Then Henschel mounted his great Flemish horse an' I had to hand the child up to him. After that he said: Good-bye, an' rode off.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: An' father just stood there an' looked on?

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: What was he goin' to do about it? The whole village might ha' turned out for all the good it would ha' done. When once Henschel lays his hands on somethin'—I wouldn't advise nobody to cross him! An' there's no one in the county that likes to pick a quarrel with him neither! Your father, he didn't know what was goin' on. Then suddenly, o' course, he roared like fury an' cried out an' cursed more'n enough. But the people just laughed. They knew Henschel. An' he—Henschel—he just said reel quiet: Good luck to you, father Schäl; I'm takin' her along. The mother is waitin' for her at home. Stop drinkin'! he said, an' maybe there'll be a place with us for you some day, too.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Good-bye, I think I'll maybe drop in to-morrow.
[Exit.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: An' so he thinks I'm goin' to keep her here. I'll never do that—never in the world. She's no child o' mine! How would I be lookin' before people? First in Quolsdorf, then here! Didn't I work an' worry enough? Day an' night, you might say, I was busy with Gustel. An' now the weary trouble is to begin all over again. That'd be fine, wouldn't it? He'd better take care!

p.hi: HENSCHEL appears in the middle door. He is also clad in leathern breeches, fur jacket, tall boots, etc., just as he has dismounted. He leads by the hand a little girl of six—ragged and unwashed.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Almost merrily referring to HANNE'S last words, which he has overheard.] Who's to take care?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: —Oh, I don't know!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Look, Hanne, look who comes here! [To the child.] Go ahead, Berthel, an' say good evenin'. Go on an' say it! Say: Good evenin', mama!

p.hi: BERTHEL leaving HENSCHEL unwillingly and walks, encouraged by friendly little shoves from him, diagonally across the room to where HANNE, assuming a disgruntled attitude, sits on the bench.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [To the child, who stands helplessly before her.] What do you want here?

div.head: BERTHEL
div.p: I rode on such a pitty horsie?

p.hi: HENSCHEL and WALTHER laugh heartily.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Well now we'll keep her here. Hallo, Hanne! Are you angry about anythin'?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: You are sayin' you wouldn't be back till Monday. There's not a bite for supper in the house now.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: There'll be a bit o' bread an' bacon.
[He hangs up his cap.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Pulling ungently at BERTHEL'S clothes.] How'd you get this way?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: You'll soon have to buy her somethin' to put on! She's got hardly nothin' on her little body. 'Twas a good thing I had plenty o' blankets along, or she'd ha' been half froze on the way. [After he has removed his fur jacket and warmed his hands.] Best thing would be to put her right straight in a tub.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Best thing would ha' been if you'd ha' left her where she was.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: What did you say?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Nothin'.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I thought you were sayin' somethin'.—Into the tub with her! An' then to bed! An' you might go over her head a bit! I believe she's got a little colony there. [BERTHEL cries out.] What's the matter? Don't tug at her so rough!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Oh, don't cry, girl! That'd be the last straw!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: You must be a bit friendly with her. The lass is thankful for every kind word. Be quiet, Berthel, be quiet!

div.head: BERTHEL
div.p: I want to go to father!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: You're with mother now! Mother is good!—I'm reel satisfied that we has her with us. 'Twas the highest time. A bit longer an' we might ha' had to look for her in the graveyard.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: That wasn't half as bad as you're tryin' to make out.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [In some consternation but still kindly.] What's the meanin' o' that?
[Pause.]

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: Well, good luck to you all. I'll have to be goin'.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Wait a bit an' drink a glass o' toddy.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: If there were only some rum in the house!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, you can fetch it from Wermelskirch's!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I don't want to have nothin' to do with those people!

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: No, no. I got to go home. I got no time. I got to be ridin' half an hour yet. [To HANNE.] I don't want to be a bother to you.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Who mentioned such a thing?

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: [Humorously.] Nothin'! I didn't say nothin' at all. God forbid! I won't let myself in for nothin'. You're a hard customer. Good-bye an' good luck!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Good-bye, an' don't forget a greetin' to the wife!

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: [Already from outside.] All right! Good night! I won't forget nothin'.
[Exit.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, didn't I do the right thing this time?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: What is I to say to people?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: —You're not goin' to be ashamed o' your own daughter!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Who's sayin' I is, eh? 'Tis all the same to me! You're willin' to have 'em say evil o' me. You force 'em to it! [Harshly to the child.] Here, drink this milk! An' then off to bed with you! [BERTHEL drinks.]

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Are you goin' to go on this way?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Go on how?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: With the child!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I'm not goin' to bite her; there's no fear!
[She takes the still weeping child into the little room to bed.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Speaking after her.] She's not here to be bitten. I needn't ha' brought her, you know!
[A brief pause, after which HANNE returns.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: A man can't never know how to please you. There's no gettin' along with women folks. You always acted as if….

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [With tears of rage.] That's a lie if you want to know it!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: What's a lie!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [As above.] I never bothered you about Berthel. I never so much as mentioned her to you!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I didn't say you had. Why d'you howl so? On that account, because you didn't say nothin', I wanted to help you in spite o' your silence.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: But couldn't you ha' asked? A man ought to say somethin' before he does a thing like that!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Well now, I'll tell you somethin': This is Saturday night. I hurried all I could so's to be at home again. I thought you'd meet me different! But if it's not to be, it can't be helped. Only, leave me in peace! You understand!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Nobody's robbin' you o' your peace.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: D'you hear me? I want my peace an' that's all. You brought me to that point. I didn't think nothin' but what was good doin' this thing. Gustel is dead. She won't come back no more. Her mother took her to a better place. The bed is empty, an' we're alone. Why shouldn't we take care o' the little lass? That's the way I thinks an' I'm not her father! You ought to think so all the more, 'cause you're the child's mother!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: There you are! You're beginnin' to throw it up to me this minute!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: If you don't stop I'll go to Wermelskirch an' not come back all night! D'you want to drive me out o' the house?—I'm always hopin' things'll be different, but they gets worse … worse! I thought maybe if you had your child with you, you'd learn a little sense. If these goin's on don't end soon …

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: All I say is this: If she stays in the house an' if you tell people that she's mine …

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: They all know it! I don't have to tell 'em.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Then you c'n take your oath on it—I'll run away!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Run, run all you can—all you want to! You ought to be ashamed o' yourself to the bottom o' your heart!

p.hi: The tap room in WERMELSKIRCH'S public house. A flat, whitewashed room with a door leading to the inner rooms of the house on the left. The rear wall of this room is broken, toward its middle. The opening leads to a second, smaller, oblong room. On the right wall of this second room there is a glass door leading out into the open and, farther forward, a window. On the rear wall of the main room the bar is situated, filled with square whisky-bottles, glasses, etc. The beer is also on draught there. Highly varnished tables and chairs of cherry wood are scattered about the room. A red curtain divides the two rooms. In the oblong rear room are also chairs and tables and, in the extreme background, a billiard table. Lithographs, representing mainly hunting scenes, are hung on the walls.

WERMELSKIRCH, in a dressing gown and smoking a long pipe, sits on the left, himself playing the piano. Three members of the voluntary fire-corps play billiards. In the foreground to the right HAUFFE sits brooding over a glass of whisky. He is noticeably shabby. MRS. WERMELSKIRCH, a gipsy-like, slovenly old woman, is rinsing glasses behind the bar. FRANZISKA is crouching on a window ledge at the right playing with a kitten. The waiter GEORGE is standing at the bar over a glass of beer. He has an elegant spring suit on, as well as patent-leather shoes, kid-gloves and a top-hat set far back on his head.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [Plays and sings.]

lg.l: "When I was prince in realms Arcadian,
I lived in splendour and in wealth."

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: [Who has accompanied the music by dancing gestures.] Go on, go on with, that!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [Coughing affectedly.] Can't be done! Quite hoarse! Anyhow … pshaw!… I'll try again.
"When I was prince …." [He coughs.]

lg.l: "When I was prince in realms Arcadian,
I lived in splen … I lived in splen … "!

div.p: The devil take it!

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Aw, why don't you go on? That was quite right! That was fine!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: I see myself trying! It's all over with me!

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: I don't understand you! That's the finest kind o' chamber music!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [Laughing.] Chamber music!

lg.l: Well, maybe not! I don't know the differences so well. Hallo, Miss
Franziska, what are you laughin' at?

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: I'm laughing at your beautiful patent-leather boots.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Go right ahead! You don't expect me to go barefoot. Give that man over there a glass of beer. How would you like a bit o' cordial, Miss Franziska? You're right, my boots is pretty fine ones. They cost me twenty crowns. Why not? I c'n stand the expense; I'm able to do it! In the "Sword" hotel a man c'n at least earn somethin'. To be sure, while I was at the "Star" I couldn't ha' bought no boots like this.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: So you like it better at the "Sword"?

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: I should say so! A boss like I got now, a reel good fellow—I never had before long's I've been in the business. We're like old friends—like brothers. I could say most anythin' to him!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Well, that's very different from Siebenhaar.

p.hi: FRANZISKA laughs out.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: An' that just shows you: Pride goeth before a fall. Two or three weeks an' he'll be under the hammer. Then I c'n buy myself his gold watch.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: You'd better buy the whole house!

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Not just now. You got to wait for the proper time to do a thing like that. An' anyhow, it's sold. Your health, gentlemen!… Your health, gentlemen! When you're through, I'll order more! What's the name o' the man that bought the house? Exner? Eh? He's goin' to bottle the spring water an' export it. He's goin' to rent out the hotel.—I'd rent it this minute if I had the money.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: Why don't you go to Henschel? He'll give it to you.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: That wouldn't be as much out o' the question as you thinks.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: No, that a fac'! You're on pretty good terms with the wife!
[FRANZISKA laughs aloud.]

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Well, why shouldn't I be. That there woman's not half bad. I tell you, a fellow that knows how, c'n make the women feed out o' his hand!

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: Well, if you know enough to make Mrs. Henschel feed out o' your hand, you must know your business pretty well. I'll say that for you.

p.hi: FABIG enters, the cord of his pack around his shoulders. He sits down modestly in a corner.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Well, there you are; that's what I'm tellin' you! There's pretty few that could come up to me that way. But a man has to be on the lookout, or he'd get a good beatin' an' that's all!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Well, you're not through with it yet yourself. [SIEBENHAAR enters from the left.] Where Henschel strikes down the grass stops growing. Your servant, Mr. Siebenhaar!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [Somewhat pale.] Good morning!

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: I think I'll play a game o' billiards.
[He takes up his glass and disappears behind the curtain in the rear.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [Sitting down at a table near the piano.] Weren't you just singing, Mr. Wermelskirch? Don't let me interrupt you, please.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: What? I? Singing? That's hardly possible! You know how deeply this business affects me. But if you say so it must be true. Permit me to sit down by you. Bring me a glass of beer, too, Franziska!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: When one considers that you were completely hoarse three or four years ago, you must admit that you've recuperated remarkably.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: You're quite right. But what good does it do me? I've half way crawled out of the slough. But who knows what'll happen now?

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: [Places a glass of beer before SIEBENHAAR; to WERMELSKIRCH:] I'll bring yours at once.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [Having drunk.] What do you mean by that, exactly?

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: I don't know that I can tell you very exactly what I do mean. But I feel something in my bones. I believe there'll be a change in the weather. Jesting aside—I have all kinds of omens that are familiar to an old actor. When the waters here began to do me so much good, I knew certainly that ten horses couldn't drag me away. And it wasn't a month before my road company had gone to smash. Now I suppose I'll have to wander on in the same old way again—who knows whither?

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Who knows whither? That's the way of the world. As for me—I'm not sorry!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Ah, but you're a man in the prime of life. The world has a place for a man like you everywhere. It's different with an old fellow like me. If I lose my means of making a living, I mean, if I'm given notice, what is there left me, I'd like to know? I might actually get me a hurdy-gurdy and Franziska could go about and collect the pennies.

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: That wouldn't embarrass me a bit, papa!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Not if it were to rain gold pieces!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: And, anyhow, papa, how you always talk! You could go back on the stage!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Not even at a monkey-show, girlie!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Did Mr. Exner intimate anything to you? According to what he told me he meant to leave everything pretty much as it is.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Well, I hardly belong to what could be summed up as "everything."

div.head: MRS. WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [Approaching the table in great excitement.] I must say, Mr. Siebenhaar, I must say … And you can take my word for it! I'm an old woman of fifty and I've seen a good deal of the world, but the way we've been treated here—that's really—I don't know what to call it—but it's just vulgar malice, the lowest kind of scheming, pure meanness. You can take my word for that!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Oh, mother, are you starting in too? You'd better withdraw, if you don't mind, and retire behind your barricade!

div.head: MRS. WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: I'd like to know what our little Fanny did to that woman!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: Oh, never mind, mama!

div.head: MRS. WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: On the contrary! Are we to put up with everything? Isn't one to offer any resistance if that woman robs us of our very bread—if she spreads slander about our daughter? [To SIEBENHAAR.] Did the child ever offend you in any way?

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Mama, mama! Come along now, mama, and rest a while. So! You spoke your part very well indeed. You can repeat it to-night.
[He leads her behind the bar where her sobbing is heard for some time after.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [Having resumed his seat.] She's quite right at bottom. I've heard all kinds of rumours too, to the effect that Henschel will rent the barroom. And, of course, his wife is behind that!

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: An' who else'd be back of it I'd like to know? If there's anythin' low happenin' in the village nowadays, you don't has to go an ax who's back of it! That Henschel woman's got the devil in her!

div.head: FABIG
div.p: An' she's had her eye on the barroom this long time.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [To HAUFFE.] One hardly ever sees you any longer, Hauffe? Where did you land?

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: Where d'you suppose? In misery an' hunger' An' who gave me the shove? That damned crittur of a woman! Who else'd do it, I'd like to know! I never had no trouble with Henschel!

div.head: FABIG
div.p: His wife has the breeches on—that's all!

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: I wasn't quick enough for her no more. I'm not as young as I was—that's a fac'! An' I don't go hangin' aroun' no woman's apron strings neither. An' that there is what she wants. That's what you got to do with her! She's a hot one—you might say—she don't never get enough.—But as for workin': I c'n work! Them young fellers that she hires—they're that stinkin' lazy…. I could do as much as any three of 'em.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: One feels sorry for old Henschel.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: If he's satisfied, I don't care. But he ought to know why my bones is stiff! They didn't get stiff with lazyin' aroun', an' if that man has a chest full o' money to-day, he knows who it is that helped him earn a good lot of it!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: I recall very well that you even worked for Wilhelm Henschel's father.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: Well, who else but me! That's the way it is! An' I fed Wilhelm's horses eighteen years an' more—hitched 'em up an' unhitched 'em—went on trips summer an' winter. I drove 's far's Freiburg an' 's far's Breslau: I had to drive 'way to Bromberg. Many a night I had to sleep in the waggon. I got my ears an' my hands frost bitten: I got chilblains on both feet big as pears. An' now he puts me out! Now I c'n go!

div.head: FABIG
div.p: That's all the woman's doin's: he's a good man.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: Why did he go an' load hisself with that wench! Now he can look out for hisself! An' he couldn't hardly wait to do it decent. His first wife—she wasn't hardly cold when he ran to get married to this one!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Well, no one knew her, of course.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: I knew her well enough. O Lord—that I did! If he'd ha' axed me, I could ha' told him! If he wanted to send Gustel after her mother, there wasn't no surer way for him to take: all he had to do was to make Hanne the child's step-mother.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: Ah yes, yes … well, well … I'm not sayin' nothin' more. There's many a one has shaken his head about that! But that'll be comin' home to him some day. First people just wondered; now they'd believe anythin' of him.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: That's undoubtedly mere idle talk.

p.hi: The horse dealer WALTHER enters in riding boots, hunting jacket and cap. His whip is in his hand. He sits down at one of the tables and beckons FRANZISKA to bring him beer.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: You c'n say that. Maybe it's true. But if the dead was to come back an' was to say their say—'tis old Mrs. Henschel that could tell you a thing or two. She couldn't live an' she didn't want to live! An' what's the main thing—she wasn't to live!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Hauffe, you'd better take care! If Henschel were to get wind of that …

lg.l: I wouldn't have to take care if he did! I'd say that to anyone's face.
Old Mrs. Henschel—she was meant to die! If they pisened her, I couldn't
say; I wasn't on the spot. But that thing didn't happen no natural way.
She was a well woman; she might ha' lived thirty years.

p.hi: SIEBENHAAR drinks and rises.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: I c'n bear witness that she was well. She was my own sister an' I ought to know. She was in the way an' had to go.

p.hi: SIEBENHAAR leaves quietly.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Would you like a little snuff, gentlemen? [Softly and confidentially.] And don't you think, gentlemen, that you're going a little far? It seems so to me. I wish you would watch the man. He sat here till quite late yesterday. The man sighed so pitifully—there was no one else here—that I really felt very sorry for him.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: 'Tis his bad conscience that's botherin' him!

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: Don't talk to me about Henschel! I'm sick o' hearin' about him. He an' me—we're through with each other this long time.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: No, no, Mr. Siebenhaar is right. One ought to feel sorry for him.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: He c'n think about it what he pleases. I don't care. But what I ought to think about Henschel—there's nobody that need tell me nothin' about that!

p.hi: HENSCHEL and the smith HILDEBRANT enter at the right. HENSCHEL is carrying little BERTHA, more neatly dressed than formerly, on his arm. A little pause of embarrassment falls upon the men.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Welcome, Mr. Henschel.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Good mornin', all of ye.

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: Well, Berthel, how are you?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Say thank you! Well, can't you talk?—We gets along. A body has to be satisfied. Good mornin', brother. [He stretches out his hand carelessly to WALTHER who takes it in the same fashion.] How are you? How's everythin'?

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: I gets along as usual. 'Twouldn't be bad if it was better! You're a reg'lar nurse girl nowadays!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: True, true! 'Tis almost that!

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: You're hardly ever seen without the girl. Can't you leave her with her mother?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: She's always scourin' an' workin'. The little thing is just in her way! [He sits down on a bench along the wall near the bar, not far from his brother-in-law. He keeps the little girl on his lap. HILDEBRANT sits down opposite him.] How is it, Hildebrant, what shall we have? I think we've earned a bumper o' beer? Two of 'em, then, an two glasses o' brandy.

div.head: HILDEBRANT
div.p: That son of a—actually broke my skin!

lg.l: Nothin' but a foal neither an' has the strength o'—… Good mornin',
Hauffe.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: Mornin'.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: He's a bit surly. Let's not bother him.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: Mr. Henschel, won't you buy something o' me? A needle box for the wife, maybe, or a pretty little comb to stick in the hair! [All laugh.] George, the waiter, he bought one too.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Laughing good-naturedly with the others.] Don't you come botherin' me with your trash! [To WERMELSKIRCH.] Give him a measure o' beer!—'Tis a quaint little chap he is. Who is it?

div.head: HILDEBRANT
div.p: 'Tis Fabig from Quolsdorf, I think—the most mischievous little scamp in the county.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, I got a little native from Quolsdorf here too.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: [To BERTHA.] We're good old friends, eh?

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: [To FABIG.] Why don't you dive me some nuts?

div.head: FABIG
div.p: Aha, she knows who I is! I'll look an' see if I c'n find some!

div.head: BERTHA
div.p: Outside in the waggon!

div.head: FABIG
div.p: No, they're here in my pocket! [He gives them to the child.] You see, you don't get out o' the pubs. Long ago your grandfather took you along; now you got to go about with Henschel.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [To BERTHA.] Tell him to attend to his bit o' trash! Tell him you're bein' looked out for! Tell him that!

p.hi: GEORGE comes vivaciously out of the billiard room.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: [Without noticing HENSCHEL.] Well,—I never saw the likes o' that! That there feller c'n eat glass like anythin'. Put it down on the reckoning, Miss Franziska: a lot o' beer! There's five o' us!

div.head: FRANZISKA
div.p: [Has taken BERTHA on her arm. She goes with the child behind the bar.] Bertha won't permit it; I can't do it now!

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Good heavens, Mr. Henschel, there you are too!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Without noticing GEORGE, to HILDEBRANT.] Your health, Hildebrant!
[They clink their glasses and drink.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: [To GEORGE who, a little taken aback, lights his cigar at one of the tables.] Tell me this, mister George, you're a kind of a wizard, eh?

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Well, I do declare! What makes you think so?

div.head: FABIG
div.p: 'Cause a while ago, you was gone like a light that's blown out.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: Well, what's the use o' huntin' for disagreeable things. Siebenhaar an' me—we can't agree, that's all.

div.head: FABIG
div.p: [With the gesture of boxing another's ears.] People do say that somethin' happened.—[Passing by, to HAUFFE.] Did you win in the lottery? eh?

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: You damned vermin!

div.head: FABIG
div.p: Yes, that's just what I am.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Is it true that you're working down at Nentwich's now?

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: What business is it o' yours?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Laughing and quite even-tempered.] Now look at that feller. He pricks like a weasel wherever you touches him.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: I s'pose you'll be our host here pretty soon now?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [After he has glanced at him in astonishment.] That's the first ever I've heard of it!

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: Oh, I thought! I don't know exackly who 'twas that told me.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Drinking: indifferently.] Whoever told you that must ha' been dreamin'!
[Pause.]

div.head: HILDEBRANT
div.p: In this here house everythin' is bein' turned upside down now. An' what I says is this: You'll be all sighin' to have Siebenhaar back some day.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [To HAUFFE.] You might go over to Landeshut. I got two coach horses standin' there. You might ride them in for me.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: The hell I will—that's what I'll do for you.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Laughing and calmly.] Well, now you c'n sit there till you gets blue in the face. I won't concern myself that much about you!

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: You c'n keep busy sweepin' before your own door.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: 'Tis well, 'tis well. We'll let that there be.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: You got filth enough in your own house!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Hauffe, I tell you right now: I wouldn't like to do it. But if you're goin' to start trouble here—I tell you that—I'll kick you out!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Peace, gentlemen! I beg of you: peace!

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: You're not the host here an' you can't kick nobody out! You has no more right to say anythin' here than me! I don't let you nor nobody tell me to hold my tongue. No, not you an' not your wife, no matter how you scheme, you two! That don't scare me an' don't bother me that much!

p.hi: Without any show of anger, HENSCHEL grasps HAUFFE by the chest and pushes him, struggling in vain, toward the door. Just before reaching it he turns slightly, opens the door, puts HAUFFE out, and closes it again. During this scene the following colloquy takes place:

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: Let go, I tell you! I just warn you: let go!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Mr. Henschel, that won't do; I can't permit that!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I gave you fair warnin'! There's no help for you now.

div.head: HAUFFE
div.p: Are you goin' to choke me? Let go, I tell you! You're not the host here!

div.head: MRS. WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [From behind the bar.] What's the meaning of this? That will never do, Ludwig! You can't permit yourself to be treated that way!

div.head: FABIG
div.p: [While HENSCHEL, holding HAUFFE, is rapidly approaching the door.] You might as well let it be. There's nothin' to be done. That there man—he's like an athlete. He'll bite his teeth into the edge of a table, and he'll lift the table up for you so steady, you won't notice a glass on it shakin'. If he went an' took the notion, I tell you, we'd all be flyin' out into the street different ways!

p.hi: HAUFFE has been put out, HENSCHEL returns.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Resuming his seat amid a general silence.] He wouldn't give no rest—he's that stubborn.

div.head: FIRST FIREMAN
div.p: [Who has come in out of the billiard room and drunk a glass of whisky at the bar.] I'd like to pay. A man had better go. In the end anybody might be flyin' out o' here, you know.

lg.l: Yon take another glass of beer. That would be the last straw. After all,
I am still master here.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: If that's the way you're goin' to do, Henschel, when you stands behind the bar and runs this here place instead o' Wermelskirch—you won't keep many customers, I c'n tell you that!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Customers like that don't matter.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: You won't be able to pick 'em out, though. Hauffe don't pay with counterfeit money neither.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: He c'n pay anyway he wants to, for all I care. But I tell you again now: Don't start that there business over again. I won't be takin' this place at all. If I was goin' to take it, I ought to know better than anybody else. Well, then: if I'm ready to buy a pub some day—I'll let you know! Afterward you c'n give me your advice. An' if you don't like the place an' don't patronise it—well, then, Lord A'mighty, you don't has to!

p.hi: The FIREMAN goes out slamming the door angrily behind him.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: I s'pose it's just as well to go….
[He prepares to pay his score.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Mr. Henschel, surely that isn't right of you. You drive my customers out.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, my goodness! Now tell me: If that man runs out, what has I to do with it? For my part he can stay here till mornin'.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: [Pocketing his money again.] You got no right to put anybody out o' here. You're not the host.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Anythin' else you know?

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: People knows a good deal. Only they rather keep still. Wermelskirch knows that best of all!

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Why I exactly? Now, look here, that's …

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Firmly and collectedly.] What is't you know? Out with it! One o' you knows one thing an' another another, an' altogether you don't know that much!
[Pause.]

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: [In a changed tone.] If you were only the same man you used to be! But God only knows what's gotten into you! In those days you had a standin' among men. People came from far an' wide to get your advice. An' what you said, that was—you might say—almost like the law o' the land. 'Twas like Amen in church. An' now there's no gettin' along with you!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Go right ahead with your preachin'.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: Very well, I s'pose you're noticin' it all yourself. Formerly, you had nothin' but friends. Nowadays nobody comes to you no more; an' even if they did want to come they stay away on account o' your wife. Twenty years Hauffe served you faithful. Then, suddenly, he don't suit your wife, an' you take him by the scruff an' put him out. What's the meanin' o' that! That woman has but to look at you an' you're jumpin' at her beck, instead o' goin' an' takin' a stout rope an' knockin' the wickedness out o' her!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: If you don't keep still this minute—I'll take you by the scruff too.

div.head: GEORGE
div.p: [To HENSCHEL.] Don't forget yourself, whatever you do, Mr. Henschel! That man don't know no better, you see.
[Exit rapidly into the billiard room.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: I believe, Henschel, if a man comes nowadays an' tells you the truth, you're capable o' flingin' him against the wall. But a feller like that, a worthless windbag like George—he c'n lie to you day an' night. Your wife an' he—they c'n compete with each other makin' a fool o' you! If you want to be cheated—all right! But if you got a pair o' eyes left in your head, open 'em once an' look around you an' look at that there feller good an' hard. Them two deceive you in broad daylight!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [About to hurl himself upon WALTHER, masters his rage.] What did you say—eh? Nothin'! Aw, it's all right.
[Pause.]

div.head: FABIG
div.p: It's reg'lar April weather this day. Now the sun shines an' now it blows again.

div.head: HAUFFE'S VOICE
div.p: [From without.] I'll pay you back for this! You watch out! You c'n let it be now! We'll meet again: we'll meet at court—that's where.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: [Finishes his glass.] Good-bye. I'm meanin' well by you, Henschel.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Lays his hand about WALTHER'S wrist.] You stay here! Y' understan'?

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: What is I to do here?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: You'll see for yourself. All I says is: You stay! [To FRANZISKA.] Go down an' tell my wife she's to come up!

p.hi: FRANZISKA goes.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: But, dear Mr. Henschel, I beg you, for heaven's sake, don't cause a scandal here! The police will be coming at me next, and then …

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [In an outburst of towering, withering rage—bluish-red of face.] I'll beat you all to death if Hanne don't come here—now!!!

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: [In helpless perplexity.] Wilhelm, Wilhelm, don' go an' commit some foolishness now! I wish I hadn't said nothin'. An' it didn't mean nothin'. You know yourself how people will talk!

lg.l: Wilhelm, you're a good man. Come to your senses! My God, how you look!
Think, man, think! Why, you fairly roared! What's the matter with you?
That must ha' been heard all over the house!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Anybody c'n hear me now that wants to. But you stay here an' Hanne is to come here.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: Why should I be stayin' here? I don't know what for! Your affairs—they don't concern me a bit. I don't mingle in 'em an' I don't want to!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Then you should ha' thought before you spoke!

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: Everythin' else that's between us'll be settled in court. There we'll see who's in the right. I'll get hold o' my money; never fear! Maybe you're wife'll think it over once or twice before she goes an' perjures herself. The rest don't concern me. I tell you to let me go. I has no time. I has to go to Hartau, an' I can't be kept waitin' here.

p.hi: SIEBENHAAR re-enters.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: What's happened here?

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Goodness, gracious, I don't know! I don't know what Mr. Henschel wants!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Who continues to imprison WALTHER'S wrist.] Hanne is to come here: that's all.

div.head: MRS. WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: [To SIEBENHAAR.] The men were drinking their beer quite peacefully. Suddenly Mr. Henschel came in and began a dispute as though he were master here.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [With a deprecating gesture.] All right; all right. [To HENSCHEL.] What's happened to you, Henschel?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Mr. Siebenhaar, it's no fault o' mine. I couldn't help things comin' about this way. You may think what you please, Mr. Siebenhaar. I give you my word—'twasn't my fault.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: You needn't excuse yourself to me, Henschel. I know you're a man of peace.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Yes. I was in your father's service long ago, an' even if it looks that way a thousand times over—it wasn't my fault that this here has happened. I don't know myself what I has done. I never was quarrelsome—that's certain! But now things has come about …! They scratch an' they bite at me—all of 'em! An' now this man here has said things o' my wife that he's got to prove—prove!!—or God help him!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Why don't you let the people gossip?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Proofs! Proofs! Or God help him!

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: I can prove it an' I will. There are not many people in this room that don't know it as well as I. That there woman is on an evil way. 'Tis no fault o' mine, an' I wouldn't ha' mentioned it. But I'm not goin' to let you strike me. I'm no liar. I always speaks the truth! Ask it of anybody! Ask Mr. Siebenhaar here on his honour an' conscience! The sparrows is twitterin' it on every roof—an' worse things 'n that!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Think over what you're saying carefully, Walther.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: He forces me to it! Why don't he let me go? Why is I to suffer for other people? You know it all as well as I? How did you used to stand with Henschel in other years when his first wife was alive? D'you think people don't know that? An' now you don't cross his threshold.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: The relations between us are our private affair. And I will not permit remark or interference.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: All right. But if first his wife dies, though she's as well as anybody, an' when Gustel goes an' dies eight weeks later, then, I'm thinkin' it's more'n a private affair!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: What?—Hanne is to come!

p.hi: MRS. HENSCHEL enters suddenly and quickly, just as she has come from her work and still drying her hands.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: What're you roarin' about so?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: 'Tis well that you're here.—This man here says—

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Makes a movement as if to go.] Damned rot that it …

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: You're to stay here!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL

lg.l: Are you all drunk together? What're you thinkin' of, anyhow? D'you think
I'm goin' to stay here an' play monkey tricks for you?

div.p: [She is about to go.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Hanne, I advise you … This man here says …

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Aw, he c'n say what he wants to, for all I cares!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: He says that you deceive me before my face an' behind my back!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: What? What? What? What?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: That's what he says! Is he goin' to dare to say that? An' that … my wife …

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Me? Lies! Damned lies!
[She throws her apron over her face and rushes out.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: That I … that my wife … that we together … that our Gustel … 'Tis well! 'Tis well!
[He releases WALTHER'S hand and lets his head sink, moaning, on the table.

div.head: WALTHER
div.p: I won't be made out a liar here.

p.hi: The same room as in the first three acts. It is night, but the moonlight throws a moderate brightness into the room. It is empty. Several days have passed since the occurrences in the fourth act.

A candle is lit in the small adjoining room; at the end of a few seconds HENSCHEL enters, carrying the candle in a candlestick of tin. He wears leathern breeches but his feet are cased in bedroom slippers. Slowly he approaches the table, gazes hesitatingly first backward, then toward the window, finally puts the candlestick on the table and sits down by the window. He leans his chin on his hand and stares at the moon.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Invisible, from the adjoining chamber, calls:] Husband! Husband! What are you doin' out there?—the same mortal foolishness all the time! —[She looks in, but half-clad.] Where are you? Come 'n go to bed! 'Tis time to sleep! To-morrow you won't be able to go out again! You'll be lyin' like a sack o' meal and everythin' 'll go upside down in the yard. [She comes out, half-clad as she is, and approaches HENSCHEL hesitatingly and fearfully.] What are you doin', eh?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: —Me?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Why are you sittin' there an' not sayin' a word?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I'm lookin' at the clouds.

lg.l: Oh, no, my goodness; it's enough to confuse a person's head! What's to be
seen up there, I'd like to know! The same worry, night after night.
There's no rest in the world for nobody no more. What are you starin' at?
Say somethin', won't you?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Up there!… That's where they are!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: You're dreaming, eh? You, Wilhelm, wake up! Lay down in your bed an' go to sleep. There's nothin' but clouds up there!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Anybody that has eyes c'n see what there is!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: An' anybody that gets confused in his mind goes crazy.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I'm not confused.
MRS. HENSCHEL I'm not sayin' that you are! But if you go on actin' this way, you will be!
[She shivers, pulls on a jacket, and stirs the ashes in the oven with a poker.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: What time is it?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: A quarter of two.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: You've got a watch hangin' to you; it used to hang behind the door.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: What fancies is you goin' to have next? 'Tis hangin' where it always did.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Rising.] I think I'll go over to the stables a bit.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I tells you to go to bed, or I'll raise an alarm. You got nothin' to do in the stable now! 'Tis night, an' in bed is where you belong!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Remains standing quietly and looking at HANNE.] Where's Gustel?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: What are you botherin' for? She's lyin' in bed asleep! What are you always worritin' over the girl for? She don't lack for nothin'! I don't do nothin' to her!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: She don't lack for nothin'. She's gone to bed. She's gone to sleep betimes—Gustel has. I don't mean Berthel.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Wailing, stuffs her apron into her mouth.] I'll run away! I won't stay here!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: —Go to bed, go! I'll come too. Your cryin' can't help no more now. 'Tis our Lord alone knows whose fault it is. You can't help it; you don't need to cry.—Our Lord an' me—we two, we knows.

p.hi: [He turns the key in the door.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Hastily turning it back again.] Why d'you lock the door? I won't stand bein' locked in.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I don't rightly know why I turned the key.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Them people has gone an' addled your brains for you! They'll have to answer some day for the things they've put into your head! I took as good care o' your girl as I did o' my own. She wouldn't ha' died o' that! But I can't wake the dead. If a body is to die, she dies—in this world. There's no holdin' people like that; they has to go. There never was much strength in Gustel—you know that as well as I. Why do you go axin' me an' lookin' at me as if I done God knows what to her!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Suspiciously.] Maybe you did somethin'. 'Tis not impossible.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Beside herself.] Oh, if somebody'd foretold this—I'd ha' gone beggin' my bread first. No, no, O my goodness, if I'd ha' known that! To have to listen to things like that! Didn't I want to go? An' who kept me back? Who held me fast in the house here? I could ha' made my livin' any time! I wasn't afraid; I could always work. But you didn't let up. Now I got my reward. Now I got to suffer for it!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: 'Tis true, maybe, that you has to suffer for it. Things comes as they come. What c'n a body do?
[He locks the door again.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: You're to leave the door open, Wilhelm, or I'll cry for help!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: —Sh! Keep still! Did you hear? There's somethin' runnin' along the passage. D'you hear? Now it goes to the washstand. D'you hear the splashin'? She's standin' there an' washin' herself!

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: You! Wilhelm! You're dreamin'! The wash-stand is in here!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: That's just it! I know very well! They can't deceive me. I know what I know, [Hurriedly.] That's all I say.—Come, come, let's go to bed. Time'll show.
[While he approaches the door of the next room, Mrs. HENSCHEL softly unlocks the door to the hall and slips out.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Taking down a whip from the frame of the door.] Why, that's my old Triest whip! Where does that old thing come from? I haven't seen it for over a year. That was bought in mother's time. [He listens.] What d'you say? Eh?—O' course … Certainly.—Nothin'!—Well, s'posin'! An' why not? 'Tis well!—I know what I has to do!—I won't be stubborn.—You let that be too.

p.hi: SIEBENHAAR enters by the door which is slightly ajar. By means of gestures he signifies to WERMELSKIRCH, who follows him, that the latter is to remain behind, also to MRS. HENSCHEL. He is fully clad except that he wears a silk kerchief instead of a collar. WERMELSKIRCH is in his dressing-gown.

lg.l: Good evening, Mr. Henschel! What? Are you still up? You're not well, eh?
What's the matter with you?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [After he has, for several seconds, regarded him with perplexity; simply:] I just can't sleep. I don't get sleepy at all! I'd like to take some medicine, if I knew any. I don't know how it comes. God knows!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: I'll tell you somethin', old friend: You go quietly to bed now, and to-morrow, real early, I'll send the doctor in. You must really take some serious step now.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: No doctor won't be able to help me.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: You mustn't say that; we'll see about that! Doctor Richter knows his business. My wife couldn't sleep for weeks; her head ached as if it would burst. Last Monday she took a powder, and now she sleeps all night like the dead.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Yes, yes … well, well … 'Tis possible! I'd like it well enough if I could sleep.—Is the madam reel sick?

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Oh, we're all a little under the weather. When once Monday is past, everything will straighten out again.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I s'pose you has to turn over the property on Monday.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Yes, I hope it will be possible to arrange it by Monday. In the meantime the work is heaping up so—what with writing and making the inventory—that I scarcely get out of my clothes. But come now, Henschel, and go to bed. One man has one trouble and another has another. Life is no joke and we must all see how we can best fight our way through. And even if many strange thoughts pass through your head—don't take them to heart so!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Thank you many times, Mr. Siebenhaar. Don't take anythin' in ill part, please. An' good luck to you an' your wife!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: We'll see each other again to-morrow, Henschel. You owe me no thanks for anything. We've done each other many a service in the years that we've lived together here. And those services compensate for each other. We were good friends and, surely, we will remain such.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Silently takes a few steps toward the window and looks out.]—Ah, them's queer things here. Time don't stand still in this world. Little Karl, he never came to see us no more … I can't make no objection. Maybe you was right. The lad couldn't ha' learned nothin' good here. 'Twas different—once!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Henschel, I don't know what you mean now!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: An' you didn't cross my threshold neither. 'Tis nine months since you did.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: I had too much to worry me; that's all.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Those were the very times you used to come before. No, no, I know. You were right. An' the people are right too—all of 'em. I can't take no pride in myself no more.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Henschel, you must take some rest now.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: No, no; we c'n talk about it a bit. You see, I know 'tis all my fault—I know that, an' with that we can let it be. But before I went an' took this woman—Hanne, I mean—before that it all began … slowly it began, slowly—but downhill right along. First thing, a good bonehandled whip broke. After that, I remember it right well, I drove over my dog an' he died. 'Twas the best little dog I had. Then, one right after another, three o' my horses died; an' one of 'em was the fine stallion that cost me five hundred crowns. An' then, last of all … my wife died. I noticed it well enough in my own thoughts that fate was against me. But when my wife went away from me, I had a minute in my own mind when I thought to myself: Now it's enough. There's not much else that c'n be taken from me. But you see, there was somethin' else.—I don't want to talk about Gustel. A man loses first his wife an' then a child—that's common. But no: a snare was laid for me an' I stepped into it.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Who laid a snare for you?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Maybe the devil; maybe, too, somebody else. It's throttlin' me—that's certain.
[Pause.]

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: That's a most unhappy notion of yours …

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: An' I'm denyin' nothin'. A bad man I've come to be, only it's no fault o' mine. I just, somehow, stumbled into it all. Maybe it's my fault too. You c'n say so if you want to. Who knows? I should ha' kept a better watch. But the devil is more cunnin' than me. I just kept on straight ahead.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Henschel, you're just your own worst enemy. You're fighting phantoms which have no existence at any time or place. The devil has done nothing to you, nor have you stepped into any snare. And no one is throttling you either. That is all nonsense. And such fancies are dangerous.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: We'll see; we c'n wait an' see.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Well, tell me something definite. You won't be able to do it, however you try. You are neither bad, as you say, nor are you burdened by any guilt.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Ah, I know better.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Well, what is your guilt?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Here stood the bed. An' she was lyin' in it. An' here I gave her my promise. I gave her my promise an' I've broken it!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: What promise was that?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: You know well enough!—I broke it an' when I did that, I was lost. I was done for. The game was up.—An' you see: now she can't find no rest.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Are you speaking of your dead wife?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: 'Tis of her, of her exackly that I'm speakin'. She can't find no rest in the grave. She comes an' she goes an' she finds no rest.—I curry the horses; there she stands. I take a sieve from the feed-bin, an' I see her sittin' behind the door. I mean to go to bed in the little room; 'tis she that's lyin' in the bed an' lookin' at me.—She's hung a watch aroun' my neck; she knocks at the wall; she scratches on the panes.—She puts her finger on my breast an' I'm that smothered, I has to gasp for air. No, no, I know best. You got to go through a thing like that before you know what it is. You can't tell about It. I've gone through a deal—you c'n believe me.

lg.l: Henschel, this is my last word to you: Gather all the strength you have
in you; plant yourself firmly on both legs. Go and consult a physician.
Tell yourself that you are ill, very ill, but drive these phantoms away.
They are mere cobwebs of the brain, mere fancies.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: That's what you said that there time, too. Just so or somethin' like it you said.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Very likely, and I'm willing to stand by it now. What you did in the matter of your marriage, it was your entire right to do. There was no question of any sin or guilt.

p.hi: WERMELSKIRCH steps forward.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Henschel, come over to me. We'll light the gas and play cards. We'll drink beer or whatever you want to and smoke a pipe with it; then the ghosts can come if they want to. In two hours it will be bright daylight. Then we can drink some coffee and take a walk. The devil is in this if you can't be made to be your old self again.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Maybe so; we c'n try it all right.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Well then, come along.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I won't go to your place no more.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: On account of that little nonsense the other day? That was only a misunderstanding. And all that has been cleared up. I simply won't let Hauffe come in any more. The fellow is always drunk; that's a fact. Things are often said in heat that simply enter at one ear and pass out at the other. And that's the way to treat such incidents, I always do.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: An' that'd be best too. You're quite right. But no—I won't be comin' into the barroom no more. I'm goin' to travel about a good bit, I think. Maybe they won't follow me all roun'. An' now sleep well. I'm feelin' sleepy too.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: How would it be, Henschel, if you came up with me? There's light upstairs and my office is heated. There we can all three play a little game. I wouldn't lie down to-night anyhow.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Yes, yes; we could be doin' that together. 'Tis long since I've touched a card.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: That's right. Go on up. You wouldn't be able to sleep nohow.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I'm not goin'! Y' understand me now?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Well, if you're goin' to stay, then I won't. God knows what you'll be up to this night. You'll begin to be playin' aroun' with knives again. Yes, that's what he did yesterday. A body's not sure o' her life no more.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: You won't see me goin' up there. He advised me to do what I did, an' then he was the first one to despise me for doin' it.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Henschel, I never despised you. You're an honourable fellow, through and through; don't talk nonsense now. There are certain fates that come upon men. And what one has to bear is not easy. You have grown ill, but you have remained a good man. And for that truth I'll put my hand in the fire!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Maybe that's true too, Mr. Siebenhaar.—Let it be; we'll talk about somethin' else. 'Tisn't your fault; I always said that. An' I can't blame my brother-in law neither. He knows where he gets all that from, 'Tis she herself goes roun' to people an' tells 'em. She's everywhere—now here an' now there. I s'pose she was with her brother too.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Who is it that goes about among people? Not a soul is thinking of that affair of the other night, That's quite forgotten by this time.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: It sticks to me—it does—turn it any way you please. She knows how to go about it. She's everywhere, an' she'll persuade folks. An' even, if people was goin' to be silent for my sake an' wasn't after me like so many dogs—nothin' c'n do any good. It'll stick to me.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Henschel, we won't go away until you've put that, out of your mind. You must calm, yourself entirely.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Oh, I'm sensible now an' quiet, reel quiet.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Very well. In that case we can talk quite frankly. You see for yourself how your wife repents. That waiter fellow is gone; he's far away by this time and you'll never set your eyes on him again. Anyone may fall into sin—no matter who it is. And so take each other's hands. Bury that matter, hide it out of sight and be at peace.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: I don't has to make no peace with her. [To HANNE.] I c'n give you my hand! I don't mind. That you've gone an' made a mistake—the Lord c'n judge that in this world. I won't condemn you on that account.—If only … about Gustel … if only we could know somethin' … about that … for certain!

lg.l: You c'n both kill me this minute. May I drop dead if I did any harm to
Gustel!!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: That's what I've been sayin': It'll stick to me.—Well, we c'n talk it over again to-morrow. Before we get through talkin' about that, many a drop o' water'll have time to run into the sea, I'm thinkin'.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Why don't you build a comfortable fire and cook a cup of hot coffee. After rain comes the sunshine. That's the way it is between married people. There will be storms in every marriage. But after the storm everything grows greener. The main thing is: Bye, baby, bye—[He imitates the gesture of one rocking a child in his arms.]—That's the right way. That's the thing that you two must get for yourselves. [Jovially patting HENSCHEL'S shoulder.] That's what the old man likes. You two must get together and buy a toy like that. Confound it, Henschel! It would be queer if that weren't easy. A giant of a man like you! Good night all.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Everything changes. One must have courage.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Just keep cool and dress warmly—that's it!

p.hi: SIEBENHAAR and WERMELSKIRCH withdraw. HENSCHEL goes slowly to the door and is about to lock it again.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: You're to leave that open!

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: All right; I don't mind.—What are you doin' there?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Who has been bending down before the oven, draws herself up quickly.] I'm makin' a fire. Don't you see that?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Sitting down, heavily by the table.] For my part you c'n light the lamp too.
[He pulls out the drawer of the table.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: What are you lookin' for?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Nothin'.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL

lg.l: Then you c'n push it back in. [She steps forward and shuts the drawer.]
I s'ppose you want to wake Berthel up?

div.p: [Pause.]

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Monday he's goin'. Then we'll be alone.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Who's goin' on Monday?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Siebenhaar. The Lord knows how we'll get along with the new owner.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: He's a rich man. He won't borrow money of you at least.

lg.l: —Hanne, one of us two'll have to go. One of us two. Yes, yes,'tis true.
You c'n look at me. That can't be changed.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I'm to go away? You want to drive me away?

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: We'll see about that later—who has to go! Maybe 'twill be me, an' maybe 'twill be you. If I was to go … I know this for sure—you wouldn't be scared about yourself. You're able to look after the business like a man.—But 's I said: it don't matter about me.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: If one of us has to go—I'll go. I'm still strong enough. I'll leave an' nobody needn't see me no more. The horses an' the waggons—they're all yours. You got the business from your father an' you can't go an' leave it. I'll go an' then the trouble'll be over.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: 'Tis easy sayin' that. We got to consider one thing at a time.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: There's no use in drawin' it out. What's over and done with is over.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Rising heavily and going toward the adjoining room.] An' Berthel? What's to become o' the lass?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: She'll have to go to father, over in Quolsdorf.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [At the door of the bedroom.] Let it be. To-morrow is another day. Everythin' changes, as Siebenhaar says. To-morrow, maybe, everythin' 'll look different.
[Pause.]

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: [Invisible in the next room.] Berthel is sweating all over again.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: That won't do her no harm to be sweatin' a bit. The drops are runnin' down my neck too. Oh, what a life—[She opens a window.]—a body'd rather be dead.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: What are you talkin' about? I don't understand.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Lie down on your side an' leave me alone.

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Are you comin' too?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: It's most day now.
[She winds the clock.]

div.head: HENSCHEL
div.p: Who's windin' the clock?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: You're to keep still now. If Berthel was to wake up it'd be a fine to do. She'd howl for half an hour. [She sits down at the table and leans both elbows upon it.] 'Twould be best if a body got up an' went away,

p.hi: SIEBENHAAR peers in.

div.p: SIEBENHAAR I'm lookin' in once more. Is your husband calmer now?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Yes, yes, he lay down to sleep. [She calls.] Husband! Wilhelm!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Sh! You'd better be grateful. Hurry and go to bed yourself.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: There's nothin' else left to do. I'll go an' try. [She goes to the door of the bedroom, stands still as if spellbound and listens.] Wilhelm! You might answer.—[Louder and more frightened.] Wilhelm! You're not to frighten me this way! Maybe you think I don't know that you're still awake!!—[In growing terror.]—Wilhelm, I tell you!… [BERTHEL has waked up and wails.] Berthel, you look out an' keep still! Keep still or I don't know what'll happen!—Wilhelm! Wilhelm!
[She almost shrieks.
SIEBENHAAR looks in again.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: What's the matter, Mrs. Henschel?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: I call an' call an' he don't answer!

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Are you crazy? Why do you do that?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: —'Tis so still … Somethin's happened.

div.head: SIEBENHAAR

lg.l: What?—[He takes up the candle and goes toward the bedroom door.]
Henschel, have you fallen asleep?

div.p: [He enters the bedroom.
[Pause.]

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Not daring to follow him.] What is it? What is it? What's goin' on?

p.hi: WERMELSKIRCH looks in.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Who's in there?

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: Mr. Siebenhaar.—'Tis so still. Nobody don't answer.—

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: [Very pale and holding BERTHEL on his arm hurries out of the bedroom.] Mrs. Henschel, take your child and go up to my wife.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [Already with the child in her arms.] For God's sake, what has happened?

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: You'll find that out all too soon.

div.head: MRS. HENSCHEL
div.p: [With a voice that is first repressed and at last rises to a scream.] O God, he's done hisself some harm!

p.hi: [She runs out with the child.

div.head: WERMELSKIRCH
div.p: Shall I call the doctor?

div.head: SIEBENHAAR
div.p: Too late! He could give no help here.

div.head: AUGUST KEIL.
div.p: HAHN. HEINZEL. GOLISCH. KLEINERT. Field Labourers

p.hi: A level, fertile landscape. It is a clear, warm, sunny morning in May. Diagonally from the middle to the foreground extends a path. The fields on either side are raised slightly above it. In the immediate foreground a small potato patch on which the green shoots are already visible. A shallow ditch, covered with field flowers, separates the path from the fields. To the left of the path on a slope about six feet in height an old cherry tree, to the right hazelnut and whitethorn bushes. Nearly parallel with this path, but at some distance in the background, the course of a brook is marked by willows and alder trees. Solitary groves of ancient trees add a park-like appearance to the landscape. In the background, left, from among bushes and tree-tops arise the gables and the church steeple of the village. A crucifix stands by the wayside in the foreground, right. It is Sunday.

ROSE BERND, a beautiful, vigorous peasant girl of twenty-two emerges, excited and blushing, from the bushes at the left and sits down on the slope, after having peered shyly and eagerly in all directions. Her skirt is caught up, her feet are bare, as are her arms and neck. She is busily braiding one of her long, blonde tresses. Shortly after her appearance a man comes stealthily from the bushes on the other side. It is the landowner and magistrate, CHRISTOPHER FLAMM. He, too, gives the impression of being embarrassed but at the same time amused. His personality is not undignified; his dress betrays something of the sportsman, nothing of the dandy—laced boots, hunter's hose, a leather bottle slung by a strap across his shoulder. Altogether FLAMM is robust, unspoiled, vivid and broad-shouldered and creates a thoroughly pleasant impression. He sits down on the slope at a carefully considered distance from ROSE. They look at each other silently and then break out into inextinguishable laughter.

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: [With rising boldness and delight sings ever louder and more heartily, beating time like a conductor.]

lg.l: "In heath and under greenwood tree,
There is the joy I choose for me!
I am a huntsman bold
I am a huntsman bold!"

div.head: ROSE
div.p: [Is at first frightened by his singing; then, more and more amused, her embarrassment gives way to laughter.] Oh, but Mr. Flamm …

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: [With a touch of jaunty boldness.] Sing with me, Rosie!

div.head: ROSE
div.p: Oh, but I can't sing, Mr. Flamm.

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: Ah, that isn't true, Rosie. Don't I hear you often and often singing out on the farm:

lg.l: "A huntsman from the Rhineland …" Well!
"Rides through the forest green."

div.head: ROSE
div.p: But I don't know that song a bit, Mr. Flamm.

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: You're not to say Mr. Flamm! Come now!

lg.l: "Girlie, come and move
Here to my favourite si-i-ide!"

div.head: ROSE
div.p: [Anxiously.] The people will be comin' from church in a minute, Mr. Flamm.

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: Let 'em come! [He gets up and takes his rifle from the hollow cherry tree to the left.] I'd better hang it around again anyhow. So.—And now my hat and my pipe! Good. They can come whenever they please. [He has slung his gun across his shoulder, straightened his hat which is ornamented with a cock's feather, taken a short pipe out of his pocket and put it between his lips.] Look at the wild cherries. They're thick. [He picks up a handful of them and shows them to ROSE. With heartfelt conviction:] Rosie, I wish you were my wife!

div.head: ROSE
div.p: Goodness, Mr. Flamm!

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: I do, so help me!

div.head: ROSE
div.p: [Nervously trying to restrain him] Oh no, no!

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: Rosie, give me your dear, good, faithful little paw. [He holds her hand and sits down.] By heaven, Rosie! Look here, I'm a deucedly queer fellow! I'm damned fond of my dear old woman; that's as true as …

div.head: ROSE
div.p: [Hiding her face in her arm.] You make me want to die o' shame.

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: Damned fond of her I tell you … but—[His patience snaps.]—this doesn't concern her a bit!

div.head: ROSE
div.p: [Again tempted to laugh against her will.] Oh, but how you talk, Mr. Flamm!

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: [Filled with hearty admiration of her.] Oh, you're a lovely woman! You are lovely! You see: my wife and I … that's a queer bit of business, that is. Not the kind of thing that can be straightened out in a minute. You know Henrietta … She's sick. Nine solid years she's been bedridden; at most she creeps around in a wheel chair.—Confound it all, what good is that sort o' thing to me?
[He grasps her head and kisses her passionately.

div.head: ROSE
div.p: [Frightened under his kisses.] The people are comin' from church!

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: They're not thinking of it! Why are you so worried about the people in church to-day?

div.head: ROSE
div.p: Because August's in church too.

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: That long-faced gentry is always in church! Where else should they be? But, Rosie, it isn't even half past ten yet; and when the service is over the bells ring. No, and you needn't be worried about my wife either.

div.head: ROSE
div.p: Oh, Christopher, she keeps lookin' at a body sometimes, so you want to die o' shame.

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: You don't know my old lady; that's it. She's bright; she can look through three board walls! But on that account …! She's mild and good as a lamb … even if she knew what there is between us; she wouldn't take our heads off.

div.head: ROSE
div.p: Oh, no! For heaven's sake, Mr. Flamm!

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: Nonsense, Rosie! Have a pinch, eh? [He takes snuff.] I tell you once more: I don't care about anything! [Indignantly.] What is a man like me to do? What, I ask you? No, don't misunderstand me! Surely you know how seriously I think of our affair. Let me talk ahead once in a while.

div.head: ROSE
div.p: Mr. Christie, you're so good to me …! [With a sudden ebullition of tenderness, tears in her eyes, she kisses FLAMM'S hand.] So good … but …

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: [Moved and surprised.] Good to you? No wonder! Deuce take me, Rosie. That's very little, being good to you. If I were free, I'd marry you. You see, I've lost the ordinary way in life! Not to speak of past affairs! I'm fit for … well, I wonder what I am fit for! I might have been a royal chief forester to-day! And yet, when the governor died, I went straight home and threw over my career. I wasn't born for the higher functions of society. All this even is too civilised for me. A block house, a rifle, bear's ham for supper and a load of lead sent into the breeches of the first comer—that would be …!

div.head: ROSE
div.p: But that can't be had, Mr. Flamm! And … things has got to end sometime.

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: [Half to himself.] Confound it all to everlasting perdition! Isn't there time enough left for that spindle-shanked hypocrite? Won't there be far too much left for that fellow anyway? No> girlie, I'd send him about his business.

div.head: ROSE
div.p: Oh, but I've kept him danglin' long enough. Two years an' more he's been waitin'. Now he's urgent; he won't wait any longer. An' things can't go on this way no more.

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: [Enraged.] That's all nonsense; you understand. First you worked yourself to the bone for your father. You haven't the slightest notion of what life is, and now you want to be that bookbinder's pack horse. I don't see how people can be so vulgar and heartless as to make capital out of another human being in that way! If that's all you're looking forward to, surely there's time enough.

div.head: ROSE
div.p: No, Christie … It's easy to talk that way, Mr. Flamm! But if you was put into such circumstances, you'd be thinkin' different too.—I know how shaky father's gettin'! An' the landlord has given us notice too. A new tenant is to move in, I believe! An' then it's father's dearest wish that everythin's straightened out.

div.head: FLAMM
div.p: Then let your father marry August Keil, if he's so crazy about the fellow. Why, he's positively obsessed. It's madness the way he's taken with that man!

div.head: ROSE
div.p: You're unjust, Mr. Flamm; that's all.

div.head: FLAMM
