JOHN throws herself on the sofa and stares at the ceiling.] Maybe you'd better comb yourself a bit afterwards, Jette!—It musta been mighty dusty on the train for you to be jus' covered all over with sand the way you are! [MRS. JOHN does not answer but continues staring at the ceiling.] I must go an' bring that there little feller into the light a bit.
[He goes behind the partition.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: How long has we been married, Paul?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [Plays with the rattle behind the partition. Then answers:] That was in eighteen hundred and seventy-two, jus' as I came back from the war.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Then you came to father, didn't you? An' you assoomed a grand position an' you had the Iron Cross on the left side o' your chest.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [Appears, swinging the rattle and carrying the child on its pillow. He speaks merrily.] That's so, mother. An' I got it yet. If you want to see it, I'll pin it on.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Still stretched out on the sofa.] An' then you came to me an' you said that I wasn't to be so busy all the time … goin' up an' down, runnin' upstairs an' downstairs … that I was to be a bit more easy-goin'.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: An' I'm still sayin' that same thing to-day.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: An' then you tickled me with your moustache an' kissed me right behind my left ear! An' then …

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Then it didn't take long for us to agree, eh?

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Yes, an' I laughed an', bit by bit, I looked at myself in every one o' your brass buttons. I was lookin' different then! An' then you said …

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Well, mother, you're a great one for rememberin' things, I must say!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: An' then you said: When we has a boy, an' that'll be soon, he c'n follow the flag into the field too "with God for King an' country."

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [Sings to the child, playing with the rattle.]

lg.l: "To heaven he turns his glances bold
Whence gaze the hero sires of old:
The Rhine, the Rhine, the German Rhine!"…

div.p: Well, an' now that I has a little feller like that I ain't half so keen on sendin' him to the war to be food for powder.
[He retires with the child behind the partition.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Still staring at the ceiling.] Paul, Paul! Seems as if all that was a hundred years ago!

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [Reappears from behind the partition without the child.] Not as long ago as all that.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Look here, what d'you think? How would it be if you was to take me an' the child an' go to America?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Now listen here, Jette! What's gotten into you, anyhow? What is it? Looks as if there was nothin' but ghosts aroun' me here! You know I has a good easy temper! When the workmen heave bricks at each other, I don't even get excited. An' what do they say? Paul has a comfortable nature. But now: what's this here? The sun's shinin'; it's bright daylight! I can't see nothin'; that's a fac'. But somethin's titterin' an' whisperin' an' creepin' aroun' in here. Only when I stretches out my hand I can't lay hold on nothin'! Now I wants to know what there is to this here story about the strange girl what came to the room. Is it true?

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: You heard, Paul, that the young lady didn't come back no more. An' that shows you, don't it …

div.head: JOHN
div.p: I hear what you're sayin'. But your lips is fair blue an' your eyes look as if somebody was tormentin' you.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Suddenly changing her attitude] Yes. Why do you leave me alone year in an' year out, Paul? I sits here like in a cave an' I ain't got a soul to who I c'n say what I'm thinkin'. Many a time I've sat here an' axed myself why I works an' works, why I skimps an' saves to get together a few crowns, an' find good investments for your earnin's an' try to add to 'em. Why? Was all that to go to strangers? Paul, it's you who's been the ruin o' me!
[She lays her head on the table and bursts out in sobs.

p.hi: Softly and with feline stealth BRUNO MECHELKE enters the room at this moment. He has on his Sunday duds, a sprig of lilac in his hat and a great bunch of it in his hand. JOHN drums with his fingers on the window and does not observe him.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Has gradually realised BRUNO'S presence as though he were a ghost.] Bruno, is that you?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: [Who has recognised JOHN in a flash, softly.] Sure, it's me, Jette.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Where d'you come from? What d'you want?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: I been dancin' all night, Jette! You c'n see, can't you, that I'm dam' jolly?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [Has been staring steadily at BRUNO. A dangerous pallor has overspread his face. He now goes slowly to a small cupboard, takes out an old army revolver and loads it. MRS. JOHN does not observe this.] You! Listen! I'll tell you somethin'—somethin' you forgot, maybe. There ain't no reason on God's earth why I shouldn't pull this here trigger! You scoundrel! You ain't fit to be among human bein's! I told you … las' fall it was … that I'd shoot you down if I ever laid eyes on you in my home again! Now go … or I'll … shoot. Y'understan'?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: Aw, I ain't scared o' your jelly squirter.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Who observes that JOHN, losing control of himself, is slowly approaching BRUNO with the weapon and raising it.] Then kill me too, Paul. 'Cause he's my brother.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [Looks at her long, seems to awaken and change his mind.] All right. [He replaces the revolver carefully in the cupboard.] You're right, anyhow, Jette! It's hell, Jette, that your name's got to be on the tongue of a crittur like that. All right. The powder'd be too good, too. This here little pistol's tasted the blood o' two French cavalry men! Heroes they was! An' I don't want it to drink no dirt.

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: I ain' doubtin' that there's dirt in your head! An' if it hadn't been that you board with my sister here I'd ha' let the light into you long ago, you dirt eater, so you'd ha' bled for weeks.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [With tense restraint.] Tell me again, Jette, that it's your brother.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Go, Paul, will you? I'll get him away all right! You know's well as I that I can't help it now that Bruno's my own brother.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: All right. Then I'm one too many here. You c'n bill an' coo. [He is dressed for the street as it is and hence proceeds to go. Close by BRUNO he stands still.] You scamp! You worried your father into his grave. Your sister might better ha' let you starve behind some fence rather'n raise you an' litter the earth with another criminal like you. I'll be back in half an hour! But I won't be alone. I'll have the sergeant with me!
[JOHN leaves by the outer door, putting on his slouch hat.

p.hi: So soon as JOHN has disappeared BRUNO turns and spits out after him toward the door.

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: If I ever gets hold o' you!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Why d'you come, Bruno? Tell me, what's the matter?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: Tin's what you gotta give me. Or I'll go to hell.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Locks and latches the outer door.] Wait till I close the door! Now, what's the matter? Where d'you come from? Where has you been?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: Oh, I danced about half the night an' then, about sunrise, I went out into the country for a bit.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Did Quaquaro see you comin' in, Bruno? Then you better look out that you ain't walked into no trap.

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: No danger. I crossed the yard an' then went through the cellar o' my friend what deals in junk an' after that up through the loft.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Well, an' what happened?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: Don' fool aroun', Jette. I gotta have railroad fare. I gotta take to my heels or I'll go straight to hell.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: An' what did you do with that there girl?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: Oh, I found a way, Jette!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: What's the meanin' o' that?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: Oh, I managed to make her a little more accommodatin' all right!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: An' is it a sure thing that she won't come back now?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: Sure. I don' believe that she'll come again! But that wasn't no easy piece of work, Jette. But I tell you … gimme somethin' to drink—quick!… I tell you, you made me thirsty with your damned business—thirsty, an' hot as hell.
[He drains a jug full of water.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: People saw you outside the door with the girl.

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: I had to make a engagement with Arthur. She didn't want to have nothin' to do with me. But Arthur, he came dancin' along in his fine clothes an' he managed to drag her along to a bar. She swallowed the bait right down when he told her as how her intended was waitin' for her there. [He trills out, capering about convulsively.]

lg.l: "All we does in life's to go
Up an' down an' to an' fro
From a tap-room to a show!"

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Well, an' then?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: Then she wanted to get away 'cause Arthur said that her intended had gone off! Then I wanted to go along with her a little bit an' Arthur an' Adolph, they came along. Next we dropped in the ladies' entrance at Kalinich's an' what with tastin' a lot o' toddy an' other liquors she got good an' tipsy. An' then she staid all night with a woman what's Arthur's sweetheart. All next day there was always two or three of us boys after her, didn't let her go, an' played all kinds o' tricks, an' things got jollier an' jollier.
[The church bells of the Sunday morning services begin to ring.

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: [Goes on.] But the money's gone. I needs crowns an' pennies, Jette.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Rummaging for money.] How much has you got to have?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: [Listening to the bells.] What?

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Money!

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: The old bag o' bones in the junk shop downstairs was thinkin' as how I'd better get across the Russian frontier! Listen, Jette, how the bells is ringin'.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Why do you has to get acrost the frontier?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: Take a wet towel, Jette, an' put a little vinegar on it. I been bothered with this here dam' nosebleed all night.
[He presses his handkerchief to his nose.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Breathing convulsively, brings a towel.] Who was it scratched your wrist into shreds that way?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: [Listening to the bells.] Half past three o'clock this mornin' she could ha' heard them bells yet.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: O Jesus, my Saviour! That ain't true! That can't noways be possible! I didn't tell you nothin' like that, Bruno! Bruno, I has to sit down. Oh! [She sits down.] That's what our father foretold to me on his dyin' bed.

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: It ain't so easy jokin' with me. If you go to see Minna, jus' tell her that I got the trick o' that kind o' thing an' that them goin's on with Karl an' with Fritz has to stop.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: But, Bruno, if they was to catch you!

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: Well, then I has to swing, an' out at the Charity hospital they got another stiff to dissect.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Giving him money.] Oh, that ain't true. What did you do, Bruno?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: You're a crazy old crittur, Jette.—[He puts his hand on her not without a tremor of emotion.] You always says as how I ain't good for nothin'. But when things can't go on no more, then you needs me, Jette.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Well, but how? Did you threaten the girl that she wasn't to let herself be seen no more? That's what you ought to ha' done, Bruno! An' did you?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: I danced with her half the night. An' then we went out on the street. Well, a gentleman came along, y'understan'? Well, when I told him that I had some little business o' my own to transact with the lady an' pulled my brass-knuckles outa my breeches, o' course he took to his heels.—Then I says to her, says I: Don't you be scared. If you're peaceable an' don' make no outcry an' don' come no more to my sister axin' after the child—well, we c'n make a reel friendly bargain. So she toddled along with me a ways.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Well, an' then?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: Well, she didn't want to! An' all of a sudden she went for my throat that I thought it'd be the end o' me then an' there! Like a dawg she went for me hot an' heavy! An' then … then I got a little bit excited too—an' then, well … that's how it come …

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Sunk in horror.] What time d'you say it was?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: It must ha' been somewhere between three an' four. The moon had a big ring aroun' it. Out on the square there was a dam' cur behind the planks what got up an' howled. Then it began to drip an' soon a thunderstorm came up.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Changed and with sudden self-mastery.] It's all right. Go on. She don' deserve no better.

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: Good-bye. I s'pose we ain't goin' to see each other for years an' years.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Where you goin' to?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: First of all I gotta lie flat on my back for a couple o' hours. I'm goin' to Fritz's. He's got a room for rent in the old police station right acrost from the Fisher's Bridge. I'm safe there all right. If there's anythin' of a outcry you c'n lemme know.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Don' you want to take a peek at the child onct more?

div.head: BRUNO
div.p: [Trembling.] Naw!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Why not?

lg.l: No, Jette, not in this here life! Good-bye, Jette. Hol' on a minute: Here
I got a horseshoe. [He puts a horseshoe on the table.] I found it.
That'll bring you good luck. I don' need it.

p.hi: Stealthily as he has come, BRUNO MECHELKE also disappears. MRS. JOHN, her eyes wide with horror, stares at the spot where he stood. Then she totters backward a few paces, presses her hands, clenched convulsively as if in prayer, against her mouth, and collapses, still trying in vain to stammer out a prayerful appeal to heaven.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: I ain't no murderer! I ain't no murderer! I didn't want that to happen!

p.hi: JOHN'S room. MRS. JOHN is asleep on the sofa. WALBURGA and SPITTA enter from the outer hall. The loud playing of a military band is heard from the street.

div.head: SPITTA
div.p: No one is here.

div.head: WALBURGA
div.p: Oh, yes, there is, Erich. Mrs. John! She's asleep here.

div.head: SPITTA
div.p: [Approaching the sofa together with WALBURGA.] Is she asleep? So she is! I don't understand how anyone can sleep amidst this noise.

p.hi: The music of the band trails off into silence.

div.head: WALBURGA
div.p: Oh, Erich, sh! I have a perfect horror of the woman. Can you understand anyhow why policemen are guarding the entrance downstairs and why they won't let us go out into the street? I'm so awfully afraid that, maybe, they'll arrest us and take us along to the station.

div.head: SPITTA
div.p: Oh, but there's not the slightest danger, Walburga! You're seeing ghosts by broad daylight.

div.head: WALBURGA
div.p: When the plain clothes man came up to you and looked at us and you asked him who he was and he showed his badge under his coat, I assure you, at that moment, the stairs and the hall suddenly began to go around with me.

div.head: SPITTA
div.p: They're looking for a criminal, Walburga. It is a so-called raid that is going on here, a kind of man hunt such as the criminal police is at times obliged to undertake.

div.head: WALBURGA
div.p: And you can believe me, too, Erich, that I heard papa's voice. He was talking quite loudly to some one.

div.head: SPITTA
div.p: You are nervous. You may have been mistaken.

div.head: WALBURGA
div.p: [Frightened at MRS. JOHN, who is speaking in her sleep.] Listen to her: do!

div.head: SPITTA
div.p: Great drops of sweat are standing on her forehead. Come here! Just look at the rusty old horseshoe that she is clasping with both hands.

div.head: WALBURGA
div.p: [Listens and starts with fright again.] Papa!

div.head: SPITTA
div.p: I don't understand you. Let him come, Walburga. The essential thing is that one knows what one wants and that one has a clean conscience. I am ready. I long for the explanation to come about.

p.hi: A loud knocking is heard at the door.

div.head: SPITTA
div.p: [Firmly.] Come in!

p.hi: MRS. HASSENREUTER enters, more out of breath than usual. An expression of relief comes over her face as she catches sight of her daughter.

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: Thank God! There you are, children! [Trembling, WALBURGA throws herself into her mother's arms.] Girlie, but what a fright you've given your old mother.
[A pause in which only the breathing of MRS. HASSENREUTER is heard.

div.head: WALBURGA
div.p: Forgive me, mama: I couldn't act differently.

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: Oh, no! One doesn't write letters containing such thoughts to one's own mother. And especially not to a mother like me. If your soul is in pain you know very well that you can always count on me for help and counsel. I'm not a monster, and I was young myself once. But to threaten to drown yourself … and things like that … no, that's all wrong. You shouldn't have done that. Surely you agree with me, Mr. Spitta. And now this very minute … heavens, how you both look!… this very minute you must both come home with me!—What's the matter with Mrs. John?

div.head: WALBURGA
div.p: Oh yes, help us! Don't forsake us! Take us with you, mama! Oh, I'm so glad that you're here! I was just paralysed with fright!

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: Very well, then. Come along. That would be the last straw if one had to be prepared for such desperate follies from you, Mr. Spitta, or from this child! At your age one should have courage. If everything doesn't go quite smoothly you have no right to think of expedients by which one has nothing to gain and everything to lose. We live but once, after all.

div.head: SPITTA
div.p: Oh, I have courage! And I'm not thinking of putting an end to myself as one who is weary and defeated … unless Walburga is refused to me. In that case, to be sure, my determination is firm. It doesn't in the least undermine my belief in myself or in my future that I am poor for the present and have to take my dinner occasionally in the people's kitchen. And I am sure Walburga is equally convinced that a day must come that will indemnify us for all the dark and difficult hours of the present.

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: Life is long; and you're almost children to-day. It's not so very bad for a student to have to take an occasional meal in the people's kitchen. It would be much worse, however, for Walburga as a married woman. And I hope for the sake of you both that you'll wait till something in the nature of a hearthstone of your own with the necessary wood and coal can be founded. In the meantime I've succeeded in persuading papa to a kind of truce. It wasn't easy and it might have been impossible had not this morning's mail brought the news of his definitive appointment as manager of the theatre at Strassburg.

div.head: WALBURGA
div.p: [Joyously.] Oh, mama, mama! That is a ray of sunshine, isn't it?

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Sits up with a start.] Bruno!

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: [Apologising.] Oh, we've wakened you, Mrs. John.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Is Bruno gone?

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: Who? Who's Bruno?

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Why, Bruno! Don' you know Bruno?

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: Ah, yes, yes! That's the name of your brother.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Was I asleep?

div.head: SPITTA
div.p: Fast asleep. But you cried out aloud in your sleep just now.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Did you see, Mr. Spitta, how them boys out in the yard threw stones at my little Adelbert's wee grave? But I got after 'em, eh? An' they wasn't no bad slaps neither what I dealt out.

lg.l: It seems that you've been dreaming of your first little boy who died,
Mrs. John.
No, no; all that's fac'! I ain't been dreamin'. An' then I took little
Adelbert an' I went with him to the registrar's office.

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: But if your little boy's no longer alive … how could you …

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Aw, when a little child is onct born, it don't matter if it's dead … it's still right inside o' its mother. Did you hear that dawg howlin' behind the board fence? An' the moon had a big ring aroun' it! Bruno, you ain' doin' right!

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: [Shaking MRS. JOHN.] Wake up, my good woman! Wake up, Mrs. John! You are ill! Your husband ought to take you to see a physician.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Bruno, you ain' doin' right! [The bells are ringing again.] Ain't them the bells?

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: The service is over, Mrs. John.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Wholly awake now, stares about her.] Why does I wake up? Why didn't you take an ax when I was asleep an' knock me over the head with it?—What did I say? Sh! Only don't tell a livin' soul a word, Mrs. Hassenreuter.
[She jumps up and arranges her hair by the help of many hairpins.

p.hi: Manager HASSENREUTER appears in the doorway.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: [Starting at the sight of his family.]
"Behold, behold, Timotheus, Here are the cranes of Ibicus!"

Didn't you tell me there was a shipping agent's office in the neighbourhood, Mrs. John?—[To WALBURGA.] Ah, yes, my child! While, with the frivolousness of youth you have been thinking of your pleasure and nothing but your pleasure, your papa has been running about for three whole hours again purely on business.—[To SPITTA.] You wouldn't be in such a hurry to establish a family, young man, if you had the least suspicion how hard it is—a struggle from day to day—to get even the wretched, mouldy necessary bit of daily bread for one's wife and child! I trust it will never be your fate to be suddenly hurled one day, quite penniless, into the underworld of Berlin and be obliged to struggle for a naked livelihood for yourself and those dear to you, breast to breast with others equally desperate, in subterranean holes and passages! But you may all congratulate me! A week from now we will be in Strassburg. [MRS. HASSENREUTER, WALBURGA and SPITTA all press his hand.] Everything else will be adjusted.

lg.l: You have fought an heroic battle for us during these past years, papa.
And you did it without stooping to anything unworthy.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: It was a fight like that of drowning men who struggle for planks in the water. My noble costumes, made to body forth the dreams of poets, in what dens of vice, on what reeking bodies have they not passed their nights—odi profanum vulgus—only that a few pennies of rental might clatter in my cashbox! But let us turn to more cheerful thoughts. The freight waggon, alias the cart of Thespis is at the door in order to effect the removal of our Penates to happier fields—[Suddenly turning to SPITTA.] My excellent Spitta, I demand your word of honour that, in your so-called despair, you two do not commit some irreparable folly. In return I promise to lend my ear to any utterances of yours characterised by a modicum of good sense.—Finally: I've come to you, Mrs. John, firstly because the officers bar all the exits and will permit no one to go out; and secondly because I would like exceedingly to know why a man like myself, at the very moment when his triumphant flag is fluttering in the wind again, should have become the object of a malicious newspaper report!

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: Dear Harro, Mrs. John doesn't understand you.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: Aha! Then let us begin ab ovo. I have letters here [he shows a bundle of them] one, two, three, five—about a dozen! In these letters unknown but malicious individuals congratulate me upon an event which is said to have taken place in my storage loft. I would pay no attention to these communications were they not confirmed by a news item in the papers according to which a newborn infant is said to have been found in the loft of a costumer in the suburbs … a costumer, forsooth! I would have said nothing, I repeat, if this item had not perplexed me. Undoubtedly there is a case of mistaken identity involved here. In spite of that, I don't like to have the report stick to me. Especially since this cub of a reporter speaks of the costumer as being a bankrupt manager of barn stormers. Read it, mama: "The Stork Visits Costumer." I'll box that fellow's ears! This evening my appointment at Strassburg is to be made public in the papers and at the same time I am to be offered as a kind of comic dessert urbi et orbi. As if it were not obvious that of all curses that of being made ridiculous is the worst!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: You say there's policemen at the door downstairs, sir?

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: Yes, and their watch is so close that the funeral procession of Mrs. Knobbe's baby has been brought to a standstill. They won't even let the little coffin and the horrid fellow from the burial society who is carrying it go out to the carriage.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: What child's funeral was that?

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: Don't you know? It's the little son of Mrs. Knobbe which was brought up to me in so mysterious a way by two women and died almost under my very eyes, probably of exhaustion. À propos …

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: The Knobbe woman's child is dead?

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: À propos, Mrs. John, I was going to say that you ought really to know how the affair of those two half-crazy women who got hold of the child finally ended?

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Well now, tell me, ain't it like the very finger of God that they didn't take my little Adelbert an' that he didn't die?

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: Just why? I don't understand the logic of that. On the other hand, I have been asking myself whether the confused speeches of the Polish girl, the theft committed in my loft, and the milk bottle which Quaquaro brought down in a boot—whether all these things had not something to do with the notice in the papers.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: No, there ain't no connection between them things. Has you seen Paul, sir?

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: Paul? Ah yes; that's your husband. Yes, yes. Indeed I saw him in conversation with detective Puppe, who visited me too in connection with the theft.

p.hi: JOHN enters.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Well, Jette, wasn't I right? This here thing's happened soon enough!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: What's happened?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: D'you want me to go an' earn the thousand crowns' reward what's offered accordin' to placards on the news pillars by the chief o' police's office for denouncin' the criminal?

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: How's that?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Don't you know that all this manoeuverin' o' police an' detectives is started on account o' Bruno?

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: How so? Where? What is it? What's been started?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: The funeral's been stopped an' two o' the mourners—queer customers they is, too—has been taken prisoner. Yes, sir! That's the pass things has come to, Mr. Hassenreuter. I'm a man, sir, what's tied to a women as has a brother what's bein' pursued by the criminal police an' by detectives because he killed a woman not far from the river under a lilac bush.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: But my dear Mr. John: God forbid that that be true!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: That's a lie! My brother don' do nothin' like that.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Aw, don' he though, Jette? Mr. Hassenreuter, I was sayin' the other day what kind of a brother that is! [He notices the bunch of lilacs and takes it from the table.] Look at this here! That there monster's been in my home! If he comes back I'll be the first one that'll take him, bound hand an' foot, an' deliver him up to justice!
[He searches through the whole room.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: You c'n tell dam' fools there's such a thing as justice. There ain't no justice, not even in heaven. There wasn't a soul here. An' that bit o' lilac I brought along from Hangelsberg where a big bush of it grows behind your sister's house.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Jette, you wasn't at my sister's at all. Quaquaro jus' told me that! They proved that at headquarters. You was seen in the park by the river …

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Lies!

div.head: JOHN
div.p: An' 'way out in the suburbs where you passed the night in a arbour!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: What? D'you come into your own house to tear everythin' into bits?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: All right! I ain't sorry that things has come to this. There ain't no more secrets between us here. I foretold all that.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: [Tense with interest.] Did that Polish girl who fought like a lioness for Mrs. Knobbe's baby the other day ever show herself again?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: She's the very one. She's the one what they pulled out o' the water this morning. An' I has to say it without bitin' my tongue off: Bruno Mechelke took that girl's life.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: [Quickly.] Then she was probably his mistress?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Ask mother! I don' know about that! That's what I was scared of; that's the reason I rather didn't come home at all no more, that my own wife was loaded down with a crowd like that an' didn't have the strength to shake it off.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: Come, children!

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Why so? You jus' stay!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: You don' has to go an' open the windows an' cry out everythin' for all the world to hear! It's bad enough if fate's brought a misfortune like that on us. Go on! Make a noise about it if you want to. But you won't see me very soon again.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: And you mean to say that that …

div.head: JOHN
div.p: That's jus' what I'll do! Jus' that! I'll call in anybody as wants to know—outa the street, offa the hall, the carpenter outa the yard, the boys an' the girls what takes their confirmation lessons—I'll call 'em all an' I'll tell 'em what a woman got into on account o' her fool love for her brother!

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: And so that good-looking girl who laid claim to the child is actually dead to-day?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Maybe she was good-lookin'. I don' know nothin' about that, whether she was pretty or ugly. But it's a fac' that she's lyin' in the morgue this day.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: I c'n tell you what she was! She was a common, low wench! She had dealin's with a Tyrolese feller that didn't want to have nothin' more to do with her an' she had a child by him. An' she'd ha' liked to kill that child while it was in her own womb. Then she came to fetch it with that Kielbacke what's been in prison eighteen months as a professional baby-killer. Whether she had any dealin's with Bruno, I don' know! Maybe so an' maybe not! An' anyhow, I don' see how it concerns me what Bruno's gone an' done.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: So you did know the girl in question, Mrs. John?

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: How so? I didn't know her a bit! I'm only sayin' what everybody as knows says about that there girl.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: You're an honourable woman: you're an honourable man, Mr. John. This matter with your wayward brother is terrible enough as a fact, but it ought not seriously to undermine your married life. Stay honest and …

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Not a bit of it! I don't stay with such people; not anywhere near 'em. [He brings his fist down on the table, taps at the walls, stamps on the floor.] Listen to the crackin'! Listen, how the plasterin' comes rumblin' down behind the wall-paper! Everything rotten here, everythin's worm eaten! Everythin's undermined by varmint an' by rats an' by mice. [He see-saws on a loose plank in the floor.] Every thin' totters! Any minute the whole business might crash down into the cellar.—[He opens the door.] Selma! Selma! I'm goin' to pull outa here before the whole thing just falls together into a heap o' rubbish!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: What do you want o' Selma?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Selma is goin' to take that child an' I'll go with 'em on the train an' take it out to my sister.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: You'll hear from me if you try that! Oh, you jus' try it!

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Is my child to be brought up in surroundin's like this, an' maybe some day be driven over the roofs with Bruno an' maybe end in the penitentiary?

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Cries out at him.] That ain't your child at all! Y'understan'?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: 'S that so? Well, we'll see if an honest man can't be master o' his own child what's got a mother that's gone crazy an' is in the hands of a crowd o' murderers. I'd like to see who's in the right there an' who's the stronger. Selma!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: I'll scream! I'll tear open the windows! Mrs. Hassenreuter, they wants to rob a mother o' her child! That's my right that I'm the mother o' my child! Ain't that my right? Ain't that so, Mrs. Hassenreuter? They're surroundin' me! They wants to rob me o' my rights! Ain't it goin' to belong to me what I picked up like refuse, what was lyin' on rags half-dead, an' I had to rub it an' knead it all I could before it began to breathe an' come to life slowly? If it wasn't for me, it would ha' been covered with earth these three weeks!

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: Mr. John, to play the part of an arbitrator between married people is not ordinarily my function. It's too thankless a task and one's experiences are, as a rule, too unhappy. But you should not permit your feeling of honour, justly wounded as, no doubt, it is, to hurry you into acts that are rash. For, after all, your wife is not responsible for her brother's act. Let her have the child! Don't increase the misery of it all by such hardness toward your wife as must hurt her most cruelly and unnecessarily.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Paul, that child's like as if it was cut outa my own flesh! I bought that child with my blood. It ain't enough that all the world's after me an' wants to take it away from me; now you gotta join 'em an' do the same! That's the thanks a person gets! Why, it's like a pack o' hungry wolves aroun' me. You c'n kill me! But you can't touch my baby!

div.head: JOHN
div.p: I comes home, Mr. Hassenreuter, only this mornin'. I comes home with all my tools on the train, jolly as c'n be. I broke off all my connections in Hamburg. Even if you don' earn so much, says I to myself, you'd rather be with your family, an' take up your child in your arms a little, or maybe take it on your knee a little! That was about the way I was thinkin'!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Paul! Here, Paul! [She goes close up to him.] You c'n tear my heart out if you want to!

lg.l: [She stares long at him, then runs behind the partition, whence her

p.hi: SELMA enters from the hall. She is dressed in mourning garments and carries a little wreath in her hand.

div.head: SELMA
div.p: What is I to do? You called me, Mr. John.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Put on your cloak, Selma. Ax your mother if you c'n go an' take a trip with me to Hangelsberg. You'll earn a bit o' money doin' it. All you gotta do is to take my child on your arm an' come along with me.

div.head: SELMA
div.p: No, I ain' goin' to touch that child no more.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Why not?

div.head: SELMA
div.p: No; I'm afraid, Mr. John! I'm that scared at the way mama an' the police lieutenant screamed at me.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Appears.] Why did they scream at you?

div.head: SELMA
div.p: [Crying vociferously.] Officer Schierke even slapped my face.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Well, I'll see about that … he oughta try that again.

div.head: SELMA
div.p: I can't tell why that Polish girl took my little brother away. If I'd known that my little brother was goin' to die, I'd ha' jumped at her throat first. Now little Gundofried's coffin stands on the stairs. I believe mama has convulsions an' is lyin' down in Quaquaro's alcove. An' me they wants to take to the charity organisation, Mrs. John.
[She weeps.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Then you c'n be reel happy. They can't treat you worse'n you was treated at home.

div.head: SELMA
div.p: An' I gotta go to court! An' maybe they'll take me to gaol!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: On account o' what?

div.head: SELMA
div.p: Because they says I took the child what the Polish girl had up in the loft an' carried it down to you.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: So a child actually was born up there.

div.head: SELMA
div.p: Certainly.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: In whose loft?

div.head: SELMA
div.p: Why, where them actors lives! It ain't none o' my business! How is I to know anythin' about it? All I c'n say is …

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: You better hurry on about your business now, Selma! You got a clean conscience! You don' has to care for what people jabber.

div.head: SELMA
div.p: An' I don' want to betray nothin' neither, Mrs. John.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [Grasps SELMA, who is about to run away, and holds her fast.] Naw, you ain't goin'! Here you stays! The truth! "I don' want to betray nothin'," you says. You heard that, too, Mrs. Hassenreuter? An' Mr. Spitta an' the young lady here heard it too. The truth! You ain't goin' to leave this here spot before I don' know the rights o' this matter about Bruno an' his mistress, an' if you people did away with that child!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Paul, I swear before God that I ain't done away with it!

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Well …? Out with what you know, girl! I been seein' for a long time that there's been some secret scheming between you an' my wife. There ain't no use no more in all that winkin' an' noddin'. Is that child dead or alive?

div.head: SELMA
div.p: No, that child is alive all right.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: The one, you mean, that you carried down here under your apron or in some such way?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: If it's dead you c'n be sure that you an' Bruno'll both be made a head shorter'n you are!

div.head: SELMA
div.p: I'm tellin' you the child is alive.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: But you said at first that you hadn't brought down any child at all.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: An' you pretend to know nothin' o' that whole business, mother? [MRS. JOHN stares at him; SELMA gazes helplessly and confusedly at MRS. JOHN.] Mother, you got rid o' the child o' Bruno an' that Polish wench an' then, when people came after it, you went an' substitooted that little crittur o' Knobbe's.

div.head: WALBURGA
div.p: [Very pale and conquering her repugnance.] Tell me, Mrs. John, what happened on that day when I so foolishly took flight up into the loft at papa's coming? I'll explain that to you later, papa. On that occasion, as became clear to me later, I saw the Polish girl twice: first with Mrs. John and then with her brother.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: You, Walburga?

div.head: WALBURGA
div.p: Yes, papa. Alice Rütterbusch was with you that day, and I had made an engagement to meet Erich here. He came to see you finally but failed to meet me because I kept hidden.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: I can't say that I have any recollection of that.

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: [To her husband.] The girl has really passed more than one sleepless night on account of this matter.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: Well, Mrs. John, if you are inclined to attach any weight to the opinion of a former jurist who exchanged the law for an artistic career only after having been plucked in his bar examination—in that case let me assure you that, under the circumstances, ruthless frankness will prove your best defense.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Jette, where did you put that there child? The head detective told me—I jus' remember it now—that they're still huntin' aroun' for the child o' the dead woman! Jette, for God's sake, don't you have 'em suspect you o' layin' hands on that there newborn child jus' to get the proofs o' your brother's rascality outa the world!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Me lay hands on little Adelbert, Paul?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Nobody ain't talkin' o' Adelbert here. [To SELMA.] I'll knock your head off for you if you don' tell me this minute what's become o' the child o' Bruno an' the Polish girl!

div.head: SELMA
div.p: Why, it's behind your own partition, Mr. John!

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Where is it, Jette?

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: I ain't goin' to tell that.

p.hi: The child begins to cry.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [To SELMA.] The truth! Or I'll turn you over to the police, y'understan'? See this rope? I'll tie you hand and foot!

div.head: SELMA
div.p: [Involuntarily, in the extremity of her fear.] It's cryin' now! You know that child well enough. Mr. John.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Me?
[Utterly at sea he looks first at SELMA, then at HASSENREUTER. Suddenly a suspicion flashes upon him as he turns his gaze upon his wife. He believes that he is beginning to understand and wavers.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Don't you let a low down lie like that take you in, Paul! It's all invented by the fine mother that girl has outa spite! Paul, why d'you look at me so?

div.head: SELMA
div.p: That's low of you, mother John, that you wants to make me out so bad now. Then I won't be careful neither not to let nothin' out! You know all right that I carried the young lady's child down here an' put it in the nice, clean bed. I c'n swear to that! I c'n take my oath on that!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Lies! Lies! You says that my child ain't my child!

div.head: SELMA
div.p: Why, you ain't had no child at all, Mrs. John!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Embraces her husband's knees.] Oh, that ain't true at all!

div.head: JOHN
div.p: You leave me alone, Henrietta! Don' dirty me with your hands!

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Paul, I couldn't do no different. I had to do that, I was deceived myself an' then I told you about it in my letter to Hamburg an' then you was so happy an' I couldn't disappoint you an' I thought: it's gotta be! We c'n has a child this way too an' then …

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [With ominous calmness.] Lemme think it over, Jette. [He goes to the chest of drawers, opens a drawer and flings the baby linen and baby dresses that he finds therein into the middle of the room.] C'n anybody understan' how week after week, an' month after month, all day long an' half the nights she could ha' worked on this trash till her fingers was bloody?

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: [Gathers up the linen and the dresses in insane haste and hides them carefully in the table drawer and elsewhere.] Paul, don' do that! You c'n do anythin' else! It's like tearin' the last rag offa my naked body!

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [Stops, grasps his forehead and sinks into a chair.] If that's true, mother, I'll be too ashamed to show my face again.
[He seems to sink into himself, crosses his arms over his head and hides his face.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: Mrs. John, how could you permit yourself to be forced into a course of so much error and deception? You've entangled yourself in the most frightful way! Come, children! Unhappily there is nothing more for us to do here.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [Gets up.] You might as well take me along with you, sir.

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: Go on! Go on! I don' need you!

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [Turning to her, coldly.] So you bargained for that there kid someway an' when its mother wanted it back you got Bruno to kill her?

div.head: MRS. JOHN
div.p: You ain't no husband o' mine! How could that be! You been bought by the police! You took money to give me up to my death! Go on, Paul, you ain't human even! You got poison in your eyes an' teeth like wolves'! Go on an' whistle so they'll come an' take me! Go on, I says! Now I see the kind o' man you is an' I'll despise you to the day o' judgment!
[She is about to run from the room when policeman SCHIERKE and QUAQUARO appear.

div.head: SCHIERKE
div.p: Hold on! Nobody can't get outa this room.

div.head: JOHN
div.p: Come right in, Emil! You c'n come in reel quiet, officer. Everything in order here an' all right.

div.head: QUAQUARO
div.p: Don't get excited, Paul! This here don' concern you!

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [With rising rage.] Did you laugh, Emil?

div.head: QUAQUARO
div.p: Man alive, why should I? Only Mr. Schierke is to take that there little one to the orphan house in a cab.

div.head: SCHIERKE
div.p: Yessir! That's right. Where is the child?

div.head: JOHN
div.p: How is I to know where all the brats offa junk heaps that witches use in their doin's gets to in the end? Watch the chimney! Maybe it flew outa there on a broomstick.

div.head: MRS. JOHN

lg.l: Paul!—Now it ain't to live! No, outa spite! Now it don' has to live!
Now it's gotta go down under the ground with me!

div.p: [With lightning-like rapidity she has run behind the partition and reappears at once with the child and makes for the door. HASSENREUTER and SPITTA throw themselves in front of the desperate woman, intent on saving the child.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: Stop! I'll interfere now! I have the right to do so at this point! Whomever the little boy may belong to—so much the worse if its mother has been murdered—it was born on my premises! Forward, Spitta! Fight for it, my boy! Here your propensities come properly into play! Go on! Careful! That's it! Bravo! Be as careful as though it were the Christ child! Bravo! That's it! You yourself are at liberty, Mrs. John. We don't restrain you. You must only leave us the little boy.

p.hi: MRS. JOHN rushes madly out.

div.head: SCHIERKE
div.p: Here you stays!

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: The woman is desperate. Stop her! Hold her!

div.head: JOHN
div.p: [With a sudden change.] Look out for mother! Mother! Stop her! Catch hold o' her! Mother! Mother!

p.hi: SELMA, SCHIERKE and JOHN hurry after MRS. JOHN. SPITTA, HASSENREUTER, MRS. HASSENREUTER and WALBURGA busy themselves about the child, which lies on the table.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: [Carefully wrapping the infant.] The horrible woman may be desperate for all I care! But for that reason she needn't destroy the child.

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: But, dearest papa, isn't it quite evident that the woman has pinned her love, silly to the point of madness as it is, to this very infant? Thoughtless and harsh words may actually drive the unhappy creature to her death.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: I used no harsh words, mama.

div.head: SPITTA
div.p: An unmistakable feeling assures me that the child has only now lost its mother.

div.head: QUAQUARO
div.p: That's true. Its father ain't aroun' an' don' want to have nothin' to do with it. He got married yesterday to the widow of a man who owned a merry-go-roun'! Its mother was no better'n she should be! An' if Mrs. Kielbacke was to take care of it, it'd die like ten outa every dozen what she boards. The way things has come aroun' now—it'll have to die too.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: Unless our Father above who sees all things has differently determined.

div.head: QUAQUARO
div.p: D'you mean Paul, the mason? Not now! No sir! I knows him! He's a ticklish customer where his honour is concerned.

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: Just look how the child lies there! It's incomprehensible! Fine linen—even lace! Neat and sweet as a doll! It makes one's heart ache to think how suddenly it has become an utterly forlorn and forsaken orphan.

div.head: SPITTA
div.p: Where I judge in Israel …

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: You would erect a monument to Mrs. John! It may well be that many an element of the heroic, much that is hiddenly meritorious, lurks in these obscure fates and struggles. But not even Kohlhaas of Kohlhaasenbrück with his mad passion for justice could fight his way through! Let us use practical Christianity! Perhaps we could permanently befriend the child.

div.head: QUAQUARO
div.p: You better keep your hands offa that!

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: Why?

div.head: QUAQUARO
div.p: Unless you're crazy to get rid o' money an' are anxious for all the worries an' the troubles you'll have with the public charities an' the police an' the courts.

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: For such things I have no time to spare, I confess.

div.head: SPITTA
div.p: Won't you admit that a genuinely tragic fatality has been active here?

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: Tragedy is not confined to any class of society. I always told you that!

p.hi: SELMA, breathless, opens the outer door.

div.head: SELMA
div.p: Mr. John! Mr. John! Oh, Mr. John!

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: Mr. John isn't here. What do you want, Selma?

div.head: SELMA
div.p: Mr. John, you're to come out on the street!

div.head: HASSENREUTER
div.p: Quiet, quiet now! What is the matter?

div.head: SELMA
div.p: [Breathlessly.] Your wife … your wife … The whole street's crowded … 'buses an' tram-cars … nobody can't get through … her arms is stretched out … your wife's lyin' on her face down there.

div.head: MRS. HASSENREUTER
div.p: Why, what has happened?

div.head: SELMA
div.p: Lord! Lord God in Heaven! Mrs. John has killed herself.
